scope: Editorial AP Language concept ontology; original teaching materials, not an official College Board ontology.

concepts.title: Rhetorical situation
concepts.definition: A text is an action in a situation: someone addresses someone else, at a particular moment, to accomplish something. Meaning emerges from the relationships among writer, audience, purpose, message, and circumstances.
concepts.insight: Begin with what the text makes available. Separate explicit context from reasonable inference. Then connect a choice to a particular audience concern; an effect is plausible, not guaranteed.
concepts.example: A student requests evening library hours from the council. Cost-conscious officials need a feasible proposal; fellow students may first need a reason to attend the hearing.
concepts.misconception: Naming six components is a starting point, not an analysis of how they interact.

project.title: One issue, three rooms
project.brief: Bring one proposal before three audiences with different power to act.
project.composition: Write a council statement, a student editorial, and a letter to affected residents about evening library access. Keep the proposal consistent while changing the grounds for support.
project.visual: Build a folding room plan; place each text where its audience would encounter it.
project.analysis: Annotate six choices whose effects depend on the room. Explain one choice that would fail elsewhere.
project.argument: Defend which audience should be addressed first and why.
project.reflection: Which adaptation changed your reasoning, rather than only your vocabulary?

practice.passage: Original fictional hearing excerpt: “Council members, your budget must balance. But the library is the only quiet room some students can reach after work. Fund two evening sessions for one term, then review attendance and cost.”

read.stem: The speaker’s proposal most directly responds to which feature of the situation?
options: Officials must balance access with limited funds.
Students prefer studying without adults.
Library staff oppose any change.
The council has already approved new hours.
rationales: The trial explicitly connects student access to the council’s budget duty.
No preference about adults is supplied.
Staff opposition is not mentioned.
The speaker is asking for approval.

write.stem: The writer wants to make the request more useful to this audience. Which addition best serves that goal?
options: An account of the library’s importance to the speaker as a child.
A claim that anyone who disagrees dislikes students.
A list of larger towns that maintain longer library hours.
A projected staffing cost and a date for reviewing the trial.
rationales: The personal history could establish investment but does not help officials evaluate the trial’s feasibility.
The accusation erases the legitimate fiscal concern.
The comparison lacks the cost and staffing context needed to evaluate this town’s proposal.
These details help officials evaluate a feasible commitment.

frq.focus: Trace how the budget constraint shapes the speaker’s choices.

concepts.title: Exigence & context
concepts.definition: Exigence is the problem or occasion that makes a response feel necessary. Context includes the broader conditions that shape what a response can mean. The immediate trigger and the surrounding circumstances can overlap, but they do different explanatory work.
concepts.insight: Ask “Why this response now?” before asking “What larger conditions make it matter?” Avoid inventing historical background the passage does not provide.
concepts.example: A vote to cut evening hours is the immediate trigger; a town’s work schedules and budget constraints are context.
concepts.misconception: The subject of a text is not automatically its exigence.

project.title: A message before and after
project.brief: Investigate how a changed moment alters a public argument.
project.composition: Write two editorials on public transit, one before and one after an explicitly fictional route closure.
project.visual: Create a two-layer timeline with removable event cards.
project.analysis: Identify how three choices change because of urgency, shared knowledge, or available action.
project.argument: Argue whether urgency justifies a different standard of evidence.
project.reflection: Which background condition stayed relevant after the trigger changed?

practice.passage: Original fictional editorial: “Yesterday the district announced that the late bus will end next month. For years, our clubs have depended on it. Before the board votes on the final budget, it should hear from students who cannot arrange a ride.”

read.stem: Which development most immediately prompts the editorial?
options: The writer’s interest in transportation.
The announced end of the late bus.
The long history of school clubs.
The general difficulty of budgeting.
rationales: The passage supplies no personal history of that interest.
The announcement creates the urgent need to respond.
This is background that explains the stakes.
That condition is broader than the immediate trigger.

write.stem: Which opening would best establish the urgency of a letter about this decision?
options: Before next week’s budget vote, consider who will lose a ride home.
The district has supported extracurricular activities for many years.
Some students enjoy several clubs.
I will discuss an important topic today.
rationales: It ties a near decision to the affected audience.
Institutional history supplies background but does not establish the urgency of the impending budget vote.
The observation does not identify the impending change.
The announcement provides no specific situation.

frq.focus: Distinguish the proposed cut from the broader circumstances that give it significance.

concepts.title: Audience & stakeholders
concepts.definition: The addressed audience is whom a text directly speaks to. A wider audience may encounter it, and stakeholders may bear its consequences without being addressed. These groups need not share knowledge, interests, or power.
concepts.insight: Infer audience from address, venue, assumed knowledge, and requested action. Explain differences within an audience instead of treating all readers as identical.
concepts.example: A letter to a principal addresses a decision-maker; students and custodians may be stakeholders in its proposal to keep classrooms open.
concepts.misconception: “Everyone” is rarely a precise account of the audience.

project.title: The absent seat
project.brief: Give a neglected stakeholder a place in a local decision.
project.composition: Draft a proposal to a decision-maker and a response from a stakeholder the proposal initially overlooks.
project.visual: Make a seating chart that shows who speaks, who decides, and who bears the costs.
project.analysis: Analyze pronouns, assumed knowledge, and the placement of testimony.
project.argument: Revise the proposal to address a legitimate stakeholder objection.
project.reflection: Whose needs could you not confidently infer, and how would you investigate them?

practice.passage: Original fictional letter: “Principal Ortiz, students can organize the exhibition, but only your office can approve evening access. Custodians would need additional paid hours. Please include them in planning before you decide.”

read.stem: Which distinction does the passage establish?
options: Students have already authorized evening access.
All groups have identical responsibilities.
The principal can authorize the event, while custodians are affected by it.
The custodians are the only intended readers.
rationales: The passage explicitly reserves approval to the office.
Their roles are differentiated.
The letter separates decision-making authority from labor consequences.
The letter directly addresses the principal.

write.stem: Which addition best accounts for an affected group’s needs?
options: Students should avoid discussing staffing.
The proposal should include staff availability and compensation.
The exhibition will be exciting for everyone.
The principal has an attractive office.
rationales: This excludes a stated stakeholder concern.
It responds to the custodians’ actual burden.
The universal claim ignores different consequences.
This detail is irrelevant to the decision.

frq.focus: Distinguish the council audience from the residents represented in the speech.

concepts.title: Purpose & message
concepts.definition: Message is what a text communicates; purpose is what the writer seeks to accomplish by communicating it. A writer may inform readers in order to change how they judge a proposal, not simply to provide facts.
concepts.insight: Use a purposeful verb and an object: “reframe repair as a practical choice” is more useful than “persuade.” Trace how local purposes contribute to the whole.
concepts.example: “The building closes at six” communicates a fact. In a hearing, that fact may support a request to extend access.
concepts.misconception: An emotional response is not always the final purpose of a text.

project.title: One fact, three purposes
project.brief: See how the same information can lead toward different actions.
project.composition: Use a clearly labeled fictional fact sheet to write a public notice, a persuasive appeal, and a reflective essay.
project.visual: Arrange the texts as three paths leaving the same factual starting point.
project.analysis: Explain how selection, sequence, and emphasis change the function of shared facts.
project.argument: Defend the ethical boundary between emphasis and distortion.
project.reflection: Where did your desired effect tempt you to omit a relevant fact?

practice.passage: Original fictional appeal: “The garden produced fewer vegetables than expected. Yet twenty neighbors learned to grow food there. If we judge it only by weight harvested, we will miss what deserves continued support.”

read.stem: The writer’s primary purpose is to
options: deny that the harvest was small.
teach readers how to grow vegetables.
argue that food production is irrelevant.
broaden the criteria used to judge the garden.
rationales: The opening explicitly acknowledges the shortfall.
No cultivation instructions are offered.
The text challenges an exclusive measure, not all concern for harvests.
The contrast asks readers to value learning as well as yield.

write.stem: Which sentence best advances the writer’s purpose?
options: We should stop recording harvests.
The garden is near a brick wall.
Next year’s review should measure both harvests and participants’ new skills.
Vegetables can be cooked in many ways.
rationales: This discards a relevant measure rather than supplementing it.
Location does not develop the stated purpose.
It turns the broader standard into a specific evaluation plan.
Cooking does not address the evaluation standard.

frq.focus: Explain how a description of access becomes a request for a specific action.

concepts.title: Writer, speaker & persona
concepts.definition: A speaker’s presented identity is a rhetorical choice. Persona is the stance or voice a text constructs; it may draw on lived experience, expertise, humility, or distance. Do not assume a textual persona reveals everything about the actual writer.
concepts.insight: Describe what the speaker claims to know and what they acknowledge not knowing. Those boundaries can shape both credibility and the relationship with readers.
concepts.example: “I have shelved books; I have never made a payroll” presents practical involvement alongside a limit on expertise.
concepts.misconception: First person does not automatically make a text unreliable, and formal language does not guarantee authority.

project.title: The expert and the learner
project.brief: Test what a speaker gains by admitting uncertainty.
project.composition: Write two accounts of learning a difficult skill: one as an experienced mentor and one as a reflective beginner.
project.visual: Create a portrait using objects and annotations rather than a face.
project.analysis: Compare how credentials, admissions, and sentence patterns construct each persona.
project.argument: Argue when disclosed uncertainty strengthens credibility.
project.reflection: Which part of your persona was supported by experience, and which part was performance?

practice.passage: Original fictional speech: “I repair bicycles, not city budgets. But every week I see children arrive with wheels bent by the same broken curb. I can describe that damage, even if I cannot price the whole street.”

read.stem: The opening admission primarily serves to
options: define the limits of the speaker’s expertise while establishing relevant experience.
withdraw the speaker’s concern about the curb.
show that only budget experts can discuss streets.
claim expertise in every aspect of road design.
rationales: The speaker distinguishes fiscal authority from direct observation.
The concern remains central.
The speaker asserts a useful role for practical knowledge.
The admission explicitly limits expertise.

write.stem: Which revision best maintains this measured persona?
options: I alone know how the city should spend its money.
The curb is probably not worth discussing.
All officials are ignorant of daily life.
My repair records can document the pattern; an engineer should assess the remedy.
rationales: The absolute claim contradicts the persona’s limits.
This abandons the speaker’s purpose.
The blanket insult replaces measured testimony with overstatement.
It pairs relevant experience with a credible limit.

frq.focus: Analyze how the volunteer’s limited authority becomes part of her credibility.

concepts.title: Claims & defensibility
concepts.definition: A claim is an assertion that an argument asks readers to accept. Claims can concern what is true, what matters, or what should be done. A defensible claim has a scope that available reasons and evidence can plausibly support.
concepts.insight: Separate the central position from supporting claims. Ask what a skeptical reader would reasonably need to see before accepting each one.
concepts.example: “The garden has twenty plots” reports a count. “The town should fund more plots” requires reasons about benefits, demand, and tradeoffs.
concepts.misconception: A strong opinion is not strong support.

project.title: A museum of disputed labels
project.brief: Make interpretive disagreement visible without disguising it as fact.
project.composition: Write three exhibit labels for one ordinary object: a factual description, a value claim, and a policy claim.
project.visual: Construct a small exhibit with evidence cards visitors can move beside the labels.
project.analysis: Explain which details support each claim and which merely describe the object.
project.argument: Defend one claim after testing it against a skeptical visitor’s objection.
project.reflection: Which claim required the greatest change in scope?

practice.passage: Original fictional editorial: “The unused courtyard receives afternoon sun. Students have requested outdoor study space. The school should install shaded seating there, provided that the accessible route remains clear.”

read.stem: Which statement is the passage’s principal claim?
options: Students should design every school facility.
The school should add seating while preserving access.
The courtyard receives sunlight.
All outdoor spaces improve learning.
rationales: The passage mentions requests, not exclusive authority.
This is the recommendation supported by the preceding observations.
This is a contextual observation, not the main recommendation.
The passage does not make that universal claim.

write.stem: Which evidence would most directly support the proposed use?
options: A survey showing unmet demand for outdoor study space during available hours.
Evidence that students enjoy outdoor sports during lunch.
A survey showing that students prefer the school’s current indoor study room.
A report that the courtyard is warmer than nearby indoor rooms.
rationales: It connects the proposed facility to a specific need.
Enjoyment of sports does not directly establish demand for an outdoor study area.
Preference for the existing indoor room could complicate, rather than support, the proposed outdoor use.
Warmth alone does not establish unmet demand for a shaded outdoor study area.

frq.prompt: Public institutions often use limited space for competing purposes. Develop an argument about the extent to which student preferences should guide the use of school spaces.
frq.focus: Make a specific claim that your evidence can defend.

concepts.title: Evidence & relevance
concepts.definition: Evidence is material used to support a claim: observations, examples, data, testimony, or textual details. Relevance asks whether the material bears on this claim; sufficiency asks whether the amount and range justify its scope.
concepts.insight: A vivid example can establish possibility without establishing frequency. Match what the evidence can show to the wording of the conclusion.
concepts.example: One student using evening hours establishes a use case. It does not establish how many residents need those hours.
concepts.misconception: More examples do not repair a mismatch between the evidence and the claim.

project.title: The evidence cabinet
project.brief: Build a visible record of what a claim can and cannot support.
project.composition: Write competing recommendations about a proposed school resource using a shared evidence collection.
project.visual: Design a cabinet with drawers labeled observation, testimony, data, and unresolved question.
project.analysis: Trace each major claim to its support and identify an unsupported inference.
project.argument: Defend which missing evidence would most change your recommendation.
project.reflection: Which piece felt persuasive before you checked its relevance?

practice.passage: Original fictional report: “Nine of twelve students interviewed after robotics practice needed the late bus. These interviews show that transportation matters to this group; they do not establish the needs of all students.”

read.stem: The final clause primarily
options: proves that most students do not need transportation.
replaces evidence with an unrelated anecdote.
limits the conclusion to the population actually studied.
shows that the interviews have no value.
rationales: No schoolwide conclusion is supported.
The clause evaluates the scope of the existing evidence.
The sample comes from one activity, not the whole school.
They remain useful evidence about this group.

write.stem: To support a schoolwide claim, the writer should add
options: an unsupported estimate of total demand.
responses from students across activities and schedules.
more descriptive adjectives about robotics.
the same interviews repeated word for word.
rationales: An estimate without a basis cannot establish the claim.
A broader sampling approach better matches the larger population.
Description does not broaden the sample.
Repetition adds no independent information.

frq.prompt: A single personal story can influence a public decision. Develop an argument about the value and limitations of personal experience as evidence in decisions affecting a community.
frq.focus: Distinguish illustrative force from representativeness.

concepts.title: Kairos & timing
concepts.definition: Kairos concerns the fitness of a response to a particular moment and setting. A writer considers when an audience can listen, what decision remains open, and which circumstances make an action possible.
concepts.insight: Distinguish the event that prompts speech from the opportunity to influence it. Urgency needs a reason: identify what changes if the audience acts later. A timely appeal can still rely on poor evidence.
concepts.example: A request to include shaded seating in a park renovation has different force before the design is approved than after construction begins.
concepts.misconception: Kairos is not simply mentioning a date or insisting that an issue is urgent. Explain why the timing changes the audience’s available choices.

project.title: The decision window
project.brief: Design an argument whose timing changes what its audience can do.
project.composition: Choose a school decision with three stages: consultation, approval, and implementation. Write a 350–500 word appeal at each stage using the same factual dossier. Specify who can still change what; label any invented details.
project.visual: Build a folding calendar with movable text panels. Use space and placement to show when each option opens or closes; provide a linear text version.
project.analysis: Compare six choices across the appeals. Explain how timing changes the grounds for action, the opening, and the scale of the request.
project.argument: Defend the most useful intervention point using the decision process as evidence. Address an advantage of acting later; revise one appeal after testing whether a reader understands the deadline.
project.reflection: When did your sense of urgency become an unsupported pressure tactic, and how did you correct it?

practice.passage: Original fictional community letter: “The park committee will approve a renovation plan on Friday. Once the paving contract is signed, adding shade will require a second excavation. Residents have asked for cooler seating for years; this week, that familiar request can still become part of the original design. Ask the committee to compare shaded and unshaded layouts before it votes. We need not pretend that one meeting will solve every access problem to recognize what this meeting can decide.”

read.stem: The reference to a second excavation primarily serves to
options: establish that the committee has deliberately ignored residents.
demonstrate that shaded seating is inexpensive to maintain.
suggest that the existing design has already been approved.
explain why making the request before approval could prevent avoidable work.
rationales: A history of requests does not establish the committee’s motives.
The passage concerns installation timing, not maintenance expenses.
The Friday vote is still in the future.
The contract creates a decision window: later changes require repeating part of the work.

write.stem: The writer wants an opening that emphasizes the audience’s present opportunity to act. Which sentence best replaces the first sentence?
options: The park committee has scheduled another meeting to discuss several matters.
Future residents will judge the park committee by the beauty of its renovation.
Before Friday’s design vote, residents can ask the committee to include shade in the initial renovation.
For generations, public parks have served as gathering places for residents.
rationales: This wording obscures both the impending vote and the relevant choice.
The prediction shifts attention to reputation without explaining what residents can do now.
This opening connects a deadline, an audience action, and the decision still available.
The broad history does not identify this decision window.

frq.focus: Explain how the impending print deadline and unresolved access problem shape the speaker’s request.

concepts.title: Genre & conventions
concepts.definition: A genre is a recurring kind of communication shaped by what a community uses it to accomplish. Conventions of structure, evidence, tone, and presentation help readers recognize how to use a text.
concepts.insight: Compare actual examples before treating a convention as a rule. Ask what work a familiar feature performs and what readers would need if you changed it. Genre can guide invention without determining every choice.
concepts.example: A closure notice helps visitors plan a route; an editorial can argue about whether the closure is justified. Both concern the same event, but they invite different kinds of reading.
concepts.misconception: Genre is more than a label such as “essay” or a fixed format. Its conventions respond to purpose, readers, and circumstances.

project.title: One event, three documents
project.brief: Translate a public decision across genres without changing the facts.
project.composition: Create a shared dossier for a fictional museum closure. Compose a 120-word visitor notice, a 450-word editorial, and a 350-word internal recommendation. Each must answer the questions its readers need answered.
project.visual: Design a document wall with three distinct reading paths. Annotate hierarchy, placement, and format; offer an accessible plain-text sequence.
project.analysis: Use six excerpts to explain how genre changes selection and ordering of evidence. Identify one convention you deliberately break and assess the cost.
project.argument: Argue which document should lead public communication. Defend your choice against another genre’s strengths, then revise the notice after a reader tries to find the closure dates and alternative access.
project.reflection: Which apparent style preference turned out to be necessary for a reader to use the document?

practice.passage: Original fictional notice and editorial: “NOTICE: The east entrance closes May 3–10 for ramp repairs. Use the west entrance on Cedar Street; a step-free route remains open.” A student editorial about the same closure begins, “A repair can improve access eventually while making it harder today. The museum should publish the temporary route wherever it advertises the exhibition.” Both texts address visitors, but they give the closure different rhetorical roles.

read.stem: Which distinction between the two texts is best supported by their wording?
options: The notice supplies immediate directions, while the editorial uses the closure to justify a communication policy.
The notice evaluates the repairs, while the editorial merely reports their schedule.
The editorial disputes the closure dates given in the notice.
The notice justifies the repair decision, while the editorial explains how to reach the entrance.
rationales: The notice identifies dates and a route; the editorial argues for publishing that route more widely.
The notice does not evaluate the repairs, and the editorial does not supply their dates.
The editorial challenges communication, not the accuracy of the dates.
This reverses their functions: the notice supplies directions, while the editorial argues for a communication change.

write.stem: The writer is revising the notice to help first-time visitors use the temporary entrance. Which addition best fits that purpose and genre?
options: The museum has long been an important site of civic conversation.
Temporary closures raise questions about the meaning of public access.
The editorial board welcomes further discussion of the repair policy.
The west entrance is beside the Cedar Street bus stop, 80 metres north of the main gate.
rationales: Institutional history does not help a visitor locate the entrance.
The abstract question belongs to a broader argument and does not resolve the immediate need.
An invitation to debate does not supply the missing route information.
A location landmark and distance make the practical directions more usable.

frq.prompt: Public institutions often communicate through familiar forms such as notices, reports, and open letters. Write an essay that argues your position on the extent to which writers should follow a genre’s conventions when communicating an unfamiliar problem.
frq.focus: Use specific examples to weigh reader expectations against the need to adapt a form.

concepts.title: Audience beliefs & values
concepts.definition: Audience adaptation begins with the commitments readers bring to a text. Shared values can support different policies; identify the reasoning that connects a value to a proposed action.
concepts.insight: Use textual evidence for audience inferences. Respect disagreement within a group.
concepts.example: Two readers value fairness but disagree about whether equal funding or need-based funding is fair.
concepts.misconception: A demographic label does not establish an individual’s beliefs.

project.title: The shared-value crossroads
project.brief: Make two reasonable policies emerge from one shared value.
project.composition: Write opposing proposals grounded in fairness, defining the term differently in each.
project.visual: Draw a branching path showing where shared commitments lead to different decisions.
project.analysis: Annotate assumptions about the audience in each proposal.
project.argument: Defend a policy using a criterion both audiences could examine.
project.reflection: What did you initially assume about the other audience?

practice.passage: Original fictional appeal: “We all want a fair competition. Equal entry fees look fair, but they exclude students who cannot pay. A fee waiver would make the opportunity to compete more equal.”

read.stem: The writer appeals to fairness by
options: denying that competition has value.
assuming all students have equal resources.
removing every competition rule.
redefining equality in terms of access.
rationales: Competition remains the shared goal.
Unequal resources motivate the proposal.
Only fees are discussed.
The argument shifts from identical fees to opportunities.

write.stem: Which addition best addresses readers worried about fair administration?
options: Anyone with concerns is selfish.
Most past winners have paid the full fee.
Use a consistent, confidential process for requesting waivers.
Fairness is whatever I prefer.
rationales: This dismisses rather than addresses the audience.
The history of winners does not establish a fair process for allocating waivers.
A clear process answers the concern without abandoning access.
This offers no shared criterion.

frq.prompt: People who share a value can disagree about what it requires. Develop an argument about the extent to which identifying shared values helps resolve public disagreements.
frq.focus: Show how a shared value produces or fails to produce agreement.

concepts.title: Ethos & credibility
concepts.definition: Ethos is the credibility a text builds with its audience. Relevant experience, accurate representation, acknowledged limits, and fair treatment of disagreement can contribute to it.
concepts.insight: Explain why a particular audience would find a particular choice credible. Credibility does not make a claim automatically true.
concepts.example: A repairer admits when an object is unsafe to fix, giving readers a reason to trust her other recommendations.
concepts.misconception: Credentials outside the relevant field are not sufficient support.

project.title: Credibility under pressure
project.brief: Construct a trustworthy public explanation of a mistake.
project.composition: Write an initial institutional statement and a revised statement after a factual error is discovered.
project.visual: Design an annotated correction notice with a visible change history.
project.analysis: Compare how admission, specificity, and accountability shape trust.
project.argument: Defend what an institution owes its audience after an error.
project.reflection: Which revision cost your speaker authority in the short term but supported trust?

practice.passage: Original fictional statement: “Our first count included duplicate entries. We have corrected the total and posted the counting method. The revised result still supports a trial, though less strongly than we initially claimed.”

read.stem: The statement builds credibility primarily through
options: transparent correction and a revised level of confidence.
insistence that the original count was perfect.
appeal to an unrelated celebrity.
concealment of the method.
rationales: The writer exposes the mistake and its consequence.
The writer acknowledges an error.
No celebrity appears.
The method is posted.

write.stem: Which addition would best strengthen this approach?
options: Remove all mention of the original error.
Promise that no future mistakes are possible.
Call critics disloyal.
Identify the independent check used to verify the revised total.
rationales: Concealment undermines transparency.
An absolute guarantee is not credible.
The attack avoids the evidence.
Verification makes the correction assessable.

frq.prompt: Publicly admitting an error can threaten a person’s authority. Develop an argument about the value of acknowledging mistakes when leading a group.
frq.focus: Distinguish appearing confident from earning warranted trust.

concepts.title: Pathos & ethical emotion
concepts.definition: Pathos engages readers’ emotions, attachments, and values. An emotional example can make a consequence concrete; it becomes misleading when it substitutes intensity for relevant support.
concepts.insight: Name the specific emotion and explain the textual mechanism that invites it. Do not assert that all readers will react identically.
concepts.example: An empty chair at a meeting may represent people excluded by its timing.
concepts.misconception: Pathos is not limited to sadness or necessarily manipulative.

project.title: An object with stakes
project.brief: Represent a community issue through an ordinary object.
project.composition: Write a narrative appeal and an evidence-focused companion about a lost public resource.
project.visual: Create an object portrait whose details reveal consequences without sensationalism.
project.analysis: Explain how pacing and concrete detail invite a particular response.
project.argument: Defend the ethical limits of using another person’s experience.
project.reflection: What emotional detail did you remove because it exceeded your evidence?

practice.passage: Original fictional appeal: “The empty music stand still bears Lina’s name. When the rehearsal bus ended, she stopped coming. Restoring a ride would mean more than filling a chair; it would let a musician return.”

read.stem: The music stand primarily functions to
options: suggest Lina dislikes music.
make an individual consequence of the bus decision tangible.
prove that every student needs a bus.
explain the mechanics of a musical instrument.
rationales: Transportation, not dislike, explains her absence.
The object connects policy to an absent participant.
One case cannot establish a universal need.
No technical explanation appears.

write.stem: Which addition would best pair the appeal with relevant support?
options: Attendance records showing which students stopped after the route ended.
A more tragic invented history presented as fact.
A count of how many students attended the last concert.
An appeal asking readers to imagine themselves in Lina’s place.
rationales: The records investigate whether the story reflects a broader pattern.
Fabrication would misrepresent the case.
Concert attendance does not establish how the bus change affected rehearsal participation.
Another emotional appeal may reinforce identification but does not supply the additional relevant evidence requested.

frq.prompt: Personal narratives often make public problems easier to understand. Develop an argument about when emotional appeals help people make responsible decisions.
frq.focus: Test the connection between emotional salience and relevant evidence.

concepts.title: Logos & sound inference
concepts.definition: Logos concerns the reasoning through which a text supports its claims. Readers must examine the evidence and the connection drawn from it; numbers and logical vocabulary alone do not establish a sound argument.
concepts.insight: Ask what must be true for this evidence to justify this conclusion. Then test that assumption.
concepts.example: More visitors during extended hours supports demand, but does not alone establish that the program is affordable.
concepts.misconception: An argument containing statistics is not necessarily logical.

project.title: The inference machine
project.brief: Make the hidden steps of a recommendation visible.
project.composition: Write two recommendations from the same small dataset, explaining each inference.
project.visual: Construct a paper machine with evidence entering one side and claims leaving the other.
project.analysis: Label the assumptions inside the machine and test a weak link.
project.argument: Defend which conclusion has the best support and narrow it if needed.
project.reflection: Which inference initially felt obvious but needed justification?

practice.passage: Original fictional report: “When the center opened on Saturdays, visits increased. Therefore the new schedule meets some demand. Whether that demand justifies the added cost requires a separate comparison.”

read.stem: The writer’s reasoning is careful because it
options: refuses to draw any conclusion.
assumes cost is irrelevant.
distinguishes evidence of use from evidence of cost-effectiveness.
treats increased visits as proof of unlimited funding.
rationales: It concludes that some demand exists.
Cost is named as a separate question.
The conclusion stops short of what the visits alone can show.
The passage explicitly avoids that leap.

write.stem: Which evidence best supports the next comparison?
options: The writer’s confidence alone.
Added operating costs alongside the number and needs of new visitors.
The number of visitors who attended before the schedule changed.
A repeated statement that visits increased.
rationales: Confidence supplies no comparative evidence.
Both costs and benefits bear on the decision.
Earlier attendance can clarify demand, but without added costs it cannot complete a cost-effectiveness comparison.
Repetition leaves the cost question unanswered.

frq.prompt: Organizations often measure success by participation. Develop an argument about the extent to which participation is a useful measure of a public program’s value.
frq.focus: Identify what a count can establish and what it leaves unresolved.

concepts.title: Defensible thesis
concepts.definition: A thesis governs an argument by answering its central question with a position that requires support. It can be qualified and may preview reasons, but it need not list three points or use a fixed sentence pattern.
concepts.insight: Test the thesis against the prompt’s actual decision. Then identify what evidence would make a reasonable reader accept it.
concepts.example: “Schools should publish grading criteria before major work because students need a usable definition of success” makes a defendable recommendation.
concepts.misconception: Complex syntax is not required for a thesis to be defensible.

project.title: The thesis gallery
project.brief: Show how evidence changes a position.
project.composition: Develop three successive theses about a school policy, then write the argument supported by the strongest version.
project.visual: Display the versions as an exhibit with evidence attached to each revision.
project.analysis: Explain changes in scope, criteria, and stakes.
project.argument: Defend the final thesis against the best version of its opposition.
project.reflection: What evidence required you to change your position rather than merely reword it?

practice.passage: Original fictional draft: “Public art generates disagreement. Some people like it, and others do not. The town must decide how to fund its next installation.”

read.stem: The draft currently lacks
options: any identifiable topic.
recognition that disagreement exists.
a reference to a decision.
a position on the decision it introduces.
rationales: Public-art funding is clearly identified.
The second sentence explicitly notes it.
The final sentence names the decision.
It describes disagreement without advancing a claim.

write.stem: Which thesis best develops a defensible position?
options: Funding decisions involve artists, residents, and town officials.
The next installation will attract many different interpretations.
The town should fund art through an open proposal process that includes residents in selection.
Public art can inspire residents, though some installations become controversial.
rationales: Naming stakeholders does not recommend how funding should be decided.
The prediction does not establish a defensible funding policy.
The recommendation can be supported and challenged.
This acknowledges effects and disagreement without taking a position on the funding decision.

frq.prompt: Communities sometimes ask residents to vote on the design of public art. Develop an argument about the extent to which public preference should determine artistic decisions in shared spaces.
frq.focus: Answer the question with a defensible criterion, not a list of opinions.

concepts.title: Evidence & commentary
concepts.definition: Commentary explains how and why evidence supports a claim. It supplies the reasoning a quotation or example cannot provide by itself. In analysis, it connects a specific choice to a purpose within a situation.
concepts.insight: After presenting evidence, articulate the inference and its significance. Repeating the example in new words is still summary.
concepts.example: A student’s inability to attend before six matters because the proposed schedule would exclude the very users the program intends to serve.
concepts.misconception: “This proves my point” does not explain a connection.

project.title: The invisible bridge
project.brief: Teach readers to inspect the reasoning between an example and a conclusion.
project.composition: Write two arguments using identical evidence but different commentary.
project.visual: Create a bridge diagram with each inferential step as a supporting beam.
project.analysis: Identify where an assumption or leap weakens one bridge.
project.argument: Revise the weaker argument with a justified connection or a narrower claim.
project.reflection: Which explanation became clearer only when you wrote the missing assumption?

practice.passage: Original fictional paragraph: “The library trial attracted workers after six. This matters because a service available only during working hours can exclude residents whose taxes help fund it.”

read.stem: The second sentence primarily
options: explains why the attendance evidence supports an access argument.
supplies a second attendance count.
contradicts the first sentence.
summarizes the library’s entire history.
rationales: It connects the observation to the principle at stake.
No additional count is given.
The sentences are compatible.
The sentence explains a present implication.

write.stem: Which addition would provide further commentary?
options: Workers attended after six.
Libraries have many books.
The trial attracted more visitors than the organizers expected.
Thus equal eligibility to use a service does not ensure a practical opportunity to use it.
rationales: This merely repeats the evidence.
The fact is unrelated to the inference.
The sentence adds another observation but does not explain the access principle connecting evidence to the claim.
This develops the implication of schedule-based exclusion.

frq.prompt: Offering everyone the same opportunity does not always ensure that everyone can use it. Develop an argument about the responsibilities of institutions to address barriers to participation.
frq.focus: Make the inference after each example explicit.

concepts.title: Paragraph development
concepts.definition: A paragraph develops a manageable part of an argument. A claim, relevant support, and commentary should work together toward a local purpose; the paragraph’s place in the larger argument matters too.
concepts.insight: Use a reverse outline: state what each sentence does, then remove or move sentences that do not advance the paragraph’s work.
concepts.example: A paragraph on access should not switch to aesthetic preferences without explaining the relationship.
concepts.misconception: A fixed number of sentences does not guarantee development.

project.title: The paragraph workshop
project.brief: Build an argument from purposeful, movable parts.
project.composition: Write three developed paragraphs supporting one recommendation; then create an alternative order.
project.visual: Make movable sentence tiles with function labels.
project.analysis: Explain how evidence and commentary cooperate within each paragraph.
project.argument: Defend the order that most effectively answers a skeptical reader.
project.reflection: Which sentence looked useful alone but disrupted the paragraph?

practice.passage: Original fictional draft: “(1) The workshop should lend tools. (2) Several participants cannot afford their own. (3) The building was painted last year. (4) A lending collection would let those participants complete projects outside class.”

read.stem: Which sentence most weakens the paragraph’s unity?
options: Sentence 4.
Sentence 3.
Sentence 1.
Sentence 2.
rationales: It explains the proposal’s consequence.
The paint detail does not develop tool access.
It states the paragraph’s claim.
It identifies the need supporting the claim.

write.stem: Which replacement for sentence 3 best develops the argument?
options: A checkout system could make a small set of tools available to many learners.
Participants say they especially enjoy the workshop’s demonstrations.
A larger classroom would allow additional people to enroll.
A tool collection can include both common and specialized equipment.
rationales: The sentence explains a workable response to the need.
Enjoying demonstrations does not explain how participants will obtain tools outside class.
Enrollment capacity is a different problem from the tool access this paragraph develops.
Listing possible contents does less to explain how the collection would solve affordability and access than a shared checkout mechanism.

frq.prompt: Shared resources can expand access but require collective responsibility. Develop an argument about the value of lending programs for items people use only occasionally.
frq.focus: Give each paragraph a distinct job in a connected argument.

concepts.title: Claims of fact, value & policy
concepts.definition: Claims of fact ask what is true, claims of value evaluate using a standard, and claims of policy recommend action. A single argument may combine all three, but each step needs its own support.
concepts.insight: Track the move from a finding to a judgment and from that judgment to a proposal. A true description does not settle what matters most or which intervention is best. Make the evaluative standard visible.
concepts.example: “The last bus leaves at six” describes a schedule. “That schedule is inadequate for evening workers” applies an access standard. “Add a seven o’clock bus” recommends a policy.
concepts.misconception: A policy claim is not proved merely by showing that a problem exists; alternatives, consequences, and feasibility still matter.

project.title: The three-claim hearing
project.brief: Build a proposal whose factual, evaluative, and practical steps can withstand separate challenges.
project.composition: Prepare three 350-word hearing briefs on a school resource: what is happening, how it should be judged, and what should change. Use at least three traceable sources or a clearly labeled common fictional dossier.
project.visual: Create a three-level evidence board with different connectors for observation, value judgment, and proposed action. Make each connector’s reasoning available in text.
project.analysis: Annotate where the briefs change claim type. Explain how six wording and organizational choices help readers recognize the standard being applied.
project.argument: Write a final recommendation that answers an objection to your chosen standard and an objection to your proposed remedy. Revise the weakest inferential link.
project.reflection: Which fact remained uncontested even when your audience rejected the policy, and what explains that disagreement?

practice.passage: Original fictional committee draft: “The computer lab closes at four, although the late activity bus leaves at five. Students waiting for that bus have no supervised place to finish digital assignments. A school that assigns online work should provide a reasonable chance to complete it on campus. The lab should remain open until the late bus departs, with staffing costs reviewed after a six-week trial.”

read.stem: The statement beginning “A school that assigns online work” primarily provides
options: a concession that the school cannot affect students’ access.
a standard that connects the described access gap to the proposed change.
a measurement of how many students use the lab.
evidence that the proposed staffing arrangement is affordable.
rationales: The statement instead assigns the school a responsibility to provide access.
It establishes a responsibility against which the current schedule can be judged.
The statement gives a value-based standard, not attendance data.
Affordability remains to be examined during the proposed review.

write.stem: Which revision of the final sentence best develops a defensible policy thesis while preserving the writer’s concern about cost?
options: The school should test supervised lab access until five for six weeks and use attendance and staffing costs to decide whether to continue.
The school’s computer lab closes before the late activity bus departs.
Digital assignments are an important part of contemporary education.
The lab must stay open until five permanently because all students will use it.
rationales: The proposal states an action and specifies criteria for evaluating it.
This reports a fact without proposing a course of action.
The general evaluation does not address the access gap or the cost concern.
This makes an unsupported prediction and removes the cost-sensitive trial.

frq.prompt: Schools and public institutions often justify a new policy by identifying an existing problem. Write an essay that argues your position on what a proposal must establish beyond the existence of a problem before an institution should adopt it.
frq.focus: Distinguish evidence of a problem, standards of judgment, and support for a particular remedy.

concepts.title: Relevance & sufficiency of evidence
concepts.definition: Relevant evidence bears on the claim being made. Sufficient evidence supports that claim’s scope and certainty. A vivid example may establish that something can happen while leaving its frequency or typicality unresolved.
concepts.insight: State the exact claim before judging the evidence. Examine population, time span, comparison, and exceptions. More examples of the same narrow kind do not automatically repair a gap in coverage.
concepts.example: One student’s missed bus can show that a schedule problem is possible. A claim that most students miss the bus needs broader records and a defined group.
concepts.misconception: Evidence is not sufficient simply because it is detailed, credible, or numerous. Its reach must match the conclusion.

project.title: The claim telescope
project.brief: Curate evidence for three claims of increasing scope.
project.composition: Choose a claim about a school space or routine. Write one paragraph showing possibility, one estimating a pattern, and one recommending a response. Use a small documented observation set or a labeled simulated dataset, and identify what each cannot establish.
project.visual: Build a paper telescope or nested-frame diagram with lenses for one case, a group, and a broader population. Attach evidence to the narrowest view it supports, and mark what remains outside each view. Include a text inventory.
project.analysis: Explain six decisions about selection, placement, and qualification. Identify a striking example you excluded because it did not support the claim.
project.argument: Defend the broadest claim your evidence warrants. Answer a proposed broader conclusion, then revise either the claim or the evidence plan rather than merely adding emphatic language.
project.reflection: Where did accumulating more of the same evidence stop improving your argument?

practice.passage: Original fictional survey memo: “Twelve members of the robotics club answered a survey after their evening meeting. Ten said the library should stay open later. These responses show that late access matters to some students whose activities end after the library closes. They do not show what most students want: club members were surveyed together, and students without after-school activities were not included.”

read.stem: The final sentence primarily limits which possible inference from the survey?
options: That the survey was conducted after an evening meeting.
That a later closing time could matter to students with activities.
That the club responses represent the preferences of the student body as a whole.
That any robotics club member wants later library hours.
rationales: The timing is stated as a fact and is not challenged.
The memo explicitly supports this possibility.
The sentence identifies missing groups and a narrow sampling setting.
Ten responses directly support that narrower observation.

write.stem: The writer wants to support the claim that interest in later hours extends beyond students in after-school clubs. Which additional evidence would be most relevant?
options: A list of awards earned by the students who completed the original survey.
Responses from a documented sample of students who do not join after-school clubs, including their reasons for wanting later access.
A second survey of the same robotics club during the next meeting.
A detailed description of the robotics club’s busiest competition week.
rationales: Academic or club achievements do not establish other students’ preferences.
This examines the specific group missing from the original evidence.
Repeated club responses do not address the excluded group.
The description adds detail about the same narrow population.

frq.prompt: A single vivid example can make a public problem visible, but decisions often require a broader evidentiary base. Write an essay that argues your position on the role an individual example should play in justifying institutional change.
frq.focus: Explain what your examples establish and where additional evidence would be needed.

concepts.title: Line of reasoning
concepts.definition: A line of reasoning is the progression of claims and explanations through which an argument earns its conclusion. It is more than the order of topics.
concepts.insight: Ask why each step must precede or follow another and how the steps jointly support the thesis.
concepts.example: A proposal establishes a need, evaluates responses, and explains why one response meets the chosen criteria.
concepts.misconception: A list of examples does not automatically form a line of reasoning.

project.title: The argument transit map
project.brief: Map an argument with more than one possible route.
project.composition: Write a recommendation and a competing route to a different conclusion using shared evidence.
project.visual: Draw a transit map with claim stations and labeled inference lines.
project.analysis: Find a station that neither route can reach without an unsupported assumption.
project.argument: Defend a revised route that addresses the gap.
project.reflection: Where did rearranging your claims change what you could conclude?

practice.passage: Original fictional argument: “Students need a quiet lunch space. The courtyard is quiet but inaccessible in rain. The unused seminar room remains available in all weather, so the school should test it first.”

read.stem: The argument proceeds by
options: rejecting the need for quiet space.
proving that every indoor room is suitable.
establishing a need, comparing options, and recommending a trial.
describing events without a recommendation.
rationales: The opening establishes that need.
Only one room is proposed for testing.
Each step supplies a reason for the next.
The final clause recommends action.

write.stem: Which addition best strengthens the reasoning before the conclusion?
options: Students generally prefer the courtyard’s appearance to that of the seminar room.
The seminar room has no scheduled lunchtime use and is reachable by an accessible route.
The courtyard has flowers.
Rain sometimes falls.
rationales: An aesthetic preference does not establish whether the room satisfies the argument’s access and weather criteria.
Availability and access test whether the option can meet the need.
This does not resolve the weather problem.
This repeats a premise without evaluating the option.

frq.prompt: A practical trial can reveal problems that planning overlooks. Develop an argument about when institutions should test a policy before adopting it permanently.
frq.focus: Build a sequence of reasons rather than a catalogue of examples.

concepts.title: Warrants & assumptions
concepts.definition: A warrant is the principle or assumption that connects support to a claim. Some warrants are shared; others are precisely what an audience disputes.
concepts.insight: State the missing “because” that makes the inference possible. Test whether the audience has reason to accept it.
concepts.example: “Students use the room, so keep it open” assumes that this use is valuable enough to justify its costs.
concepts.misconception: An unstated assumption is not automatically false.

project.title: The hidden-floor exhibition
project.brief: Expose the assumptions beneath a public recommendation.
project.composition: Write a proposal and a response from someone who accepts its facts but rejects its warrant.
project.visual: Build a transparent layered model with facts above supporting assumptions.
project.analysis: Explain where the disagreement actually occurs.
project.argument: Defend, revise, or abandon the disputed warrant.
project.reflection: Which assumption did you mistake for a fact?

practice.passage: Original fictional argument: “The workshop teaches skills that residents cannot afford to learn elsewhere. Therefore the town should subsidize it.”

read.stem: The argument depends most directly on which assumption?
options: Every workshop is already free.
Residents never learn independently.
The town has no other obligations.
Improving access to valuable learning can justify public funding.
rationales: The claim does not require this and implies costs exist.
That universal claim is unnecessary.
Competing duties can exist even if a subsidy is justified.
This principle connects the access evidence to the subsidy.

write.stem: Which addition best makes the warrant explicit?
options: The town should subsidize it because it should.
Learning occurs in many places.
Public funding is warranted when it makes an important opportunity available to people otherwise excluded.
The workshop begins on Tuesday.
rationales: This restates the conclusion circularly.
The generality does not justify this subsidy.
It supplies the principle linking need and action.
The schedule does not supply the missing principle.

frq.prompt: Public funding often supports opportunities that private markets do not make widely accessible. Develop an argument about the criteria a community should use in deciding which opportunities deserve support.
frq.focus: Make the warrant connecting your evidence to your criteria visible.

concepts.title: Induction & deduction
concepts.definition: Induction develops a probable generalization from examples or observations. Deduction applies premises to reach a conclusion that follows if the premises are true and the reasoning is valid.
concepts.insight: Evaluate sample scope in induction and both premises and form in deduction. Neither label guarantees a true conclusion.
concepts.example: Three successful trials suggest promise; they do not guarantee every future trial will succeed.
concepts.misconception: A valid deductive form can contain a false premise.

project.title: The rule-making laboratory
project.brief: Create and then stress-test a rule from observed cases.
project.composition: Write a provisional rule from five clearly documented observations and apply it to a new case.
project.visual: Design a rule tree with exceptions visibly branching from it.
project.analysis: Distinguish the inductive step from the deductive application.
project.argument: Argue whether a counterexample requires revising the rule or its conditions.
project.reflection: How did the new case expose the limits of your sample?

practice.passage: Original fictional report: “All three clubs that tried shared equipment reduced individual purchases. A lending system may therefore help other clubs, although their equipment needs could differ.”

read.stem: The reasoning is best described as
options: a qualified generalization from a small set of cases.
a proof that every club will save money.
an application of an established universal rule.
a conclusion unrelated to the evidence.
rationales: The writer extends observed results with an explicit limitation.
The qualification denies certainty.
The rule is being inferred from cases.
The evidence bears on shared equipment and purchasing.

write.stem: Which revision would make the conclusion more warranted?
options: All clubs will certainly save the same amount.
Three examples prove every possible case.
No further inquiry is possible.
A trial in clubs with similar equipment needs would test whether the benefit extends.
rationales: This exceeds the small sample.
This mistakes induction for certainty.
The limitation invites further inquiry.
The revision proposes a relevant test of generalization.

frq.prompt: People routinely generalize from a small number of experiences. Develop an argument about the conditions under which learning from experience produces reliable judgments.
frq.focus: Test representativeness and the limits of generalization.

concepts.title: Causation & consequence
concepts.definition: Causal reasoning explains how one condition contributes to another. Sequence and correlation may suggest a connection without establishing it; mechanisms and alternative explanations matter.
concepts.insight: Distinguish cause, contributing condition, and coincidence. Look for what else changed and whether the proposed mechanism is plausible.
concepts.example: Attendance rose after free admission, but a new bus route began the same week.
concepts.misconception: “After” does not necessarily mean “because of.”

project.title: The cause-and-effect mobile
project.brief: Represent a result with several interacting causes.
project.composition: Write a causal explanation and a rival explanation for a fictional change in attendance.
project.visual: Construct a hanging mobile in which moving one cause shifts the outcome.
project.analysis: Explain mechanisms, confounding factors, and uncertainty.
project.argument: Defend what additional observation would distinguish the explanations.
project.reflection: Which cause did the first visual arrangement overemphasize?

practice.passage: Original fictional report: “Visits rose after the museum removed admission fees. The same month, a new bus route began stopping outside. Either change, or both, may have contributed.”

read.stem: The final sentence acknowledges
options: certainty that transportation caused every visit.
an alternative or additional cause of the observed increase.
proof that the fee change had no effect.
a contradiction in the visit count.
rationales: The wording remains tentative.
The bus route changed alongside admission policy.
The passage leaves its effect unresolved.
No inconsistent counts appear.

write.stem: Which addition would most help evaluate the causal claim?
options: Compare attendance patterns with a similar museum where only fees changed.
Compare this museum’s attendance with its own attendance a decade earlier.
Replace “may” with “must.”
Repeat that visits rose.
rationales: A relevant comparison helps separate explanations, though it is not definitive.
A distant comparison introduces many uncontrolled changes and does not separate fees from the new bus route.
Stronger wording does not create stronger evidence.
Repetition does not isolate a cause.

frq.prompt: A policy can produce intended benefits and unanticipated consequences. Develop an argument about how decision-makers should account for uncertainty about a policy’s effects.
frq.focus: Explain mechanisms and consider a credible alternative cause.

concepts.title: Comparison & contrast
concepts.definition: Comparison develops an argument by examining cases through shared criteria. Contrast can clarify a meaningful difference, but unfair criteria or mismatched cases can distort the conclusion.
concepts.insight: Keep the basis of comparison consistent. Explain why the similarities or differences matter to the decision.
concepts.example: Compare two transit proposals on access, cost, and reliability rather than praising one’s cost and the other’s appearance.
concepts.misconception: Two things being different does not tell readers which difference matters.

project.title: The fair-comparison diptych
project.brief: Make a decision between two imperfect options.
project.composition: Write parallel evaluations of two ways to use a shared space.
project.visual: Design a diptych with the same visual scale and criteria on each side.
project.analysis: Identify how order and visual emphasis influence judgment.
project.argument: Defend a decision and acknowledge the criterion it sacrifices.
project.reflection: Which comparison initially favored your preferred option unfairly?

practice.passage: Original fictional review: “Plan A costs less initially but requires yearly repairs. Plan B costs more initially but includes five years of maintenance. Comparing purchase prices alone would hide part of the expense.”

read.stem: The comparison emphasizes the need to
options: ignore maintenance entirely.
compare only the plans’ names.
use the same time horizon when evaluating costs.
choose the highest initial price automatically.
rationales: Maintenance is the central concern.
Names do not bear on expense.
Maintenance changes the meaning of the initial price.
No automatic choice is supported.

write.stem: Which sentence best completes the comparison?
options: Future costs never matter.
Estimate each plan’s total cost over five years before deciding.
Plan A sounds friendlier.
Plan B must be best because it is expensive.
rationales: This contradicts the passage’s reasoning.
A shared period makes the criterion more consistent.
The name is irrelevant to the cost comparison.
Price alone does not establish value.

frq.prompt: People often compare the immediate cost of choices while overlooking longer-term consequences. Develop an argument about the value of considering long-term costs in community decisions.
frq.focus: Use equivalent criteria and acknowledge tradeoffs.

concepts.title: Definition & contested terms
concepts.definition: Definitions set the boundaries of an argument. A writer may define a contested term by criteria, examples, exclusions, or contrasts. Different definitions can make the same evidence support different conclusions.
concepts.insight: Test a definition against difficult cases. Ask what it includes, what it excludes, and who benefits from that boundary.
concepts.example: Defining access as “a door is open” differs from defining it as “people can practically enter and participate.”
concepts.misconception: A dictionary entry rarely resolves a dispute about how a value should operate.

project.title: The dictionary of a dispute
project.brief: Investigate one word that carries a disagreement.
project.composition: Write competing extended definitions of progress, fairness, or success, each with difficult examples.
project.visual: Create an illustrated dictionary spread with contested boundaries.
project.analysis: Analyze how examples and exclusions shape each definition.
project.argument: Defend a working definition by applying it to a counterexample.
project.reflection: Which excluded case made you reconsider your criteria?

practice.passage: Original fictional argument: “A public space is not merely land owned by the town. It is a place residents can use without a required purchase. By that measure, a plaza filled only with café tables is not fully public.”

read.stem: The writer’s definition emphasizes
options: legal ownership as the sole criterion.
the absence of all businesses nearby.
the size of the plaza.
practical use without a financial condition.
rationales: The writer explicitly rejects that limit.
Nearby businesses are not prohibited.
Size does not appear in the criteria.
The definition shifts attention from ownership to participation.

write.stem: Which example would best test this definition’s boundary?
options: A list of café menu prices.
A privately owned café that reserves its seating for customers.
A town-owned plaza with both free seating and café tables.
A private room no one claims is public.
rationales: Prices alone do not establish public access.
The case is excluded by both ownership and purchase requirements, so it does little to test the contested boundary.
The mixed case tests whether purchase-free use remains available.
This obvious exclusion does little to test the boundary.

frq.prompt: Communities often disagree about what counts as progress. Develop an argument that defines a useful standard for judging progress in a community.
frq.focus: Make your definition consequential and test a boundary case.

concepts.title: Narration & description
concepts.definition: Narration orders events; description selects details to make a subject perceptible. In argument, both can establish stakes, expose a pattern, or prepare readers for an inference.
concepts.insight: Explain why the writer includes this event or detail here. Distinguish a vivid illustration from proof of a general pattern.
concepts.example: A story about waiting outside a locked library makes a scheduling barrier visible before a policy proposal.
concepts.misconception: Retelling a story is not analyzing its argumentative function.

project.title: One minute, two meanings
project.brief: Use a small event to develop competing interpretations.
project.composition: Write two accounts of the same minute in a public place, selecting different details without changing the facts.
project.visual: Create a storyboard with an annotated camera angle for each frame.
project.analysis: Explain how sequence, omission, and focal detail guide interpretation.
project.argument: Defend which interpretation the available facts best support.
project.reflection: Which omitted detail most changed the audience’s likely judgment?

practice.passage: Original fictional essay: “At 5:59, he placed his notebook on the table. At 6:00, the closing bell sounded. He put the notebook away without opening it. The schedule had made his visit possible on paper and impossible in practice.”

read.stem: The brief narrative primarily
options: makes the difference between nominal and usable access concrete.
establishes how all visitors behave.
teaches a method for taking notes.
shows that the visitor dislikes studying.
rationales: The timed sequence shows how the policy affects one visit.
One event cannot establish universal behavior.
No note-taking instruction appears.
The closure interrupts his attempt.

write.stem: Which addition best connects this narrative to an argument?
options: The library offers a wide range of reference materials.
Everyone always arrives at closing time.
The story needs no explanation.
Hours should be evaluated in relation to when residents can actually arrive.
rationales: The collection’s breadth does not explain whether the visitor has a usable opportunity to consult it.
The claim overgeneralizes from one event.
This avoids articulating its argumentative significance.
The sentence draws a relevant policy implication.

frq.prompt: Stories can reveal aspects of a problem that numerical summaries overlook. Develop an argument about the role stories should play in evaluating public services.
frq.focus: Explain the function and limits of your examples.

concepts.title: Enthymeme & unstated premises
concepts.definition: An enthymeme is an argument that leaves part of its reasoning unstated for the audience to supply. Recovering that premise reveals both the argument’s efficiency and a possible point of disagreement.
concepts.insight: Reconstruct only the assumption needed to connect the given reason to the conclusion. Then ask whether this audience would accept it and whether its limits matter. An unstated premise is not automatically a flaw.
concepts.example: “Students pay the activity fee, so they should help choose the activities” relies on a premise linking financial contribution to a voice in decisions.
concepts.misconception: Do not invent a hidden motive when the task is to recover a premise. A premise is a proposition the inference needs, not a guess about the writer’s character.

project.title: The missing bridge workshop
project.brief: Make the invisible reasoning in a persuasive message visible.
project.composition: Write two 450-word proposals for the same school policy, one for readers who share your central premise and one for readers who question it. Include a short reconstruction of each argument as reasons, premise, and conclusion.
project.visual: Create a bridge model or flat diagram with removable premise spans. Label the consequences when a span is removed; supply a text reconstruction.
project.analysis: Quote six moments of compression or explanation. Explain which audience knowledge permits an omission and where the omission risks misreading.
project.argument: Defend your central premise with an example and a difficult exception. Revise the proposal so that the exception changes its actual scope.
project.reflection: Which omitted idea seemed obvious only because you shared it with your first audience?

practice.passage: Original fictional editorial: “Students pay an activity fee each term. They should therefore have representatives on the committee that allocates it. Representatives need not decide every purchase; staff still hold responsibility for safety and accounts. But consulting students only after the budget is settled gives contributors no meaningful influence over the activities their money supports.”

read.stem: The reasoning of the first two sentences depends most directly on which unstated premise?
options: Students have more accounting expertise than staff members.
Every activity receives the same amount of funding.
Consultation is useful only when contributors make every final decision.
People who contribute to a shared fund should have some influence over its allocation.
rationales: The editorial preserves staff responsibility for accounts and does not compare expertise.
Equal allocations are not necessary for the representation claim.
The passage explicitly permits a limited representative role.
This premise connects paying the fee to representation on the allocating committee.

write.stem: The writer wants to explain why representation would improve this particular decision process. Which addition best develops that reasoning?
options: Students are the people who pay the activity fee.
A committee with more members will necessarily reach better decisions.
Representatives could identify unmet activity needs before allocations become difficult to revise.
The committee’s allocation meetings occur once every term.
rationales: This repeats the original premise without developing its significance.
The categorical claim substitutes an unsupported rule for a mechanism.
The sentence explains a practical contribution at the point when decisions remain changeable.
The schedule alone does not explain what representation contributes.

frq.prompt: Shared assumptions can help a community act efficiently, yet those assumptions may exclude people who do not share them. Write an essay that argues your position on when a public argument should make its underlying assumptions explicit.
frq.focus: Develop a criterion for deciding which assumptions need explanation.

concepts.title: Problem–solution reasoning
concepts.definition: Problem–solution development connects an account of a problem to a proposed response. It must show how the response addresses the identified cause or barrier, using criteria that allow alternatives and tradeoffs to be assessed.
concepts.insight: Separate the visible symptom from the mechanism producing it. A solution can be partial or experimental, but it needs a plausible link to the problem. State who acts, what changes, and how success will be judged.
concepts.example: If students miss an office because its hours overlap all their classes, a clearer sign may not solve the scheduling barrier. A different opening time might.
concepts.misconception: Describing a serious problem does not establish that the writer’s preferred remedy will work or that it is the only reasonable remedy.

project.title: The repair manual for a system
project.brief: Design competing repairs for a recurring institutional obstacle.
project.composition: Document a low-stakes school process such as equipment checkout. Write a 450-word problem diagnosis and two 350-word proposals addressing different possible causes. Use observations or a labeled simulated case, not invented real-world results.
project.visual: Make an exploded diagram of the process with two replaceable repair layers. Show where each proposal changes the system and who bears its costs.
project.analysis: Analyze how six textual or visual choices establish causation, allocate responsibility, or make a proposal seem feasible. Test a version that foregrounds another cause.
project.argument: Recommend a limited pilot using explicit success and stopping criteria. Answer the strongest alternative diagnosis, then revise the proposal after a peer traces the process.
project.reflection: What evidence would persuade you that your repair targets a symptom rather than the cause?

practice.passage: Original fictional process review: “Students line up to borrow cameras while a volunteer searches a paper log for overdue equipment. Buying another camera may shorten some waits, but it will not speed that search. A shared checkout list could make current loans visible before a student reaches the desk. Test the list for two weeks, recording search time and the number of students who leave without equipment; use those results before deciding whether inventory must also grow.”

read.stem: The passage’s discussion of buying another camera primarily
options: distinguishes an inventory remedy from a response to the identified information bottleneck.
establishes that the existing inventory is sufficient for all demand.
shifts the problem from student access to the expense of equipment.
argues that record keeping matters more than whether students obtain cameras.
rationales: The writer grants a possible benefit but explains that the log search is a separate cause of delay.
The final sentence leaves open the possibility that inventory must grow.
No cost comparison is supplied; access and waiting remain central.
The proposed evaluation includes students who leave without equipment.

write.stem: The writer wants to evaluate an alternative solution using the same problem diagnosis. Which addition best serves that purpose?
options: A newer camera model would produce sharper photographs for student projects.
Students should appreciate that the existing volunteers work hard.
The shared list will eliminate every reason a student might wait.
Assigning a second volunteer to find records could also reduce search delays; compare its staffing demands with those of the shared list.
rationales: Image quality does not address the identified search delay.
The appeal does not evaluate a solution to the process problem.
The absolute prediction ignores other possible causes of waiting.
The alternative addresses the same bottleneck and introduces a relevant comparison criterion.
