frq.prompt: Institutions sometimes adopt an appealing solution before agreeing on the cause of a problem. Write an essay that argues your position on the value and limitations of testing a small intervention before committing to a larger reform.
frq.focus: Connect the design of a trial to what it can and cannot reveal.

concepts.title: Introductions & framing
concepts.definition: An introduction establishes the problem, stakes, and relationship with readers that an argument needs. It can begin with an example, distinction, question, or claim when that choice serves the situation.
concepts.insight: Evaluate what readers must understand before they can judge the thesis. An attention-getter is useful only if it advances that work.
concepts.example: A repair essay starts with a cheap toaster to expose hidden labor behind a familiar price.
concepts.misconception: A broad historical claim is not required before a focused argument.

project.title: Four doors into an argument
project.brief: Test how an opening frames a reader’s expectations.
project.composition: Write four openings for one essay, then develop two into distinct versions.
project.visual: Design four doorway panels whose visual framing matches the openings.
project.analysis: Compare the assumptions and expectations created by each entry.
project.argument: Defend the opening best suited to a skeptical audience.
project.reflection: What did your most dramatic opening make harder to explain later?

practice.passage: Original fictional draft: “(1) The repair café meets monthly. (2) Volunteers help residents assess broken objects. (3) The town should provide a permanent room because the borrowed space limits access.”

read.stem: The opening mainly provides
options: an unrelated personal digression.
basic context before a request for support.
a refutation of all objections.
a detailed cost comparison.
rationales: The context is directly relevant.
It identifies the activity that the proposal would support.
No objection is addressed.
No costs are supplied.

write.stem: Which opening best establishes the proposal’s stakes?
options: Last month, several residents left with broken objects because the borrowed room had to close early.
Residents increasingly discuss ways to reduce household waste.
The café’s volunteers bring varied skills to their repair work.
The repair café hopes to double the number of objects it accepts next year.
rationales: The example makes the space problem concrete.
The general trend is relevant but less direct evidence of the proposal’s space constraint than the closing incident.
Volunteer skills establish capacity but do not directly explain why a permanent room is needed.
The goal suggests ambition but does not establish the present room-access problem as directly as the specific closing incident.

frq.focus: Explain how the opening object prepares the essay’s larger argument.

concepts.title: Conclusions & implications
concepts.definition: A conclusion can clarify what follows from an argument, return to a meaningful image, or specify a proportionate action. It should feel earned by the reasoning already developed.
concepts.insight: Move from “what I argued” to “what this allows readers to see or do.” Do not attach an unsupported sweeping solution.
concepts.example: Returning to a repaired toaster can give a practical meaning to the essay’s claim about agency.
concepts.misconception: Repeating a thesis word for word is not the only way to conclude.

project.title: The ending changes the beginning
project.brief: Explore what an argument earns the right to ask.
project.composition: Write a full argument with three alternative endings: implication, action, and return to an image.
project.visual: Create a circular visual sequence connecting the final image to the first.
project.analysis: Explain how each ending changes the significance of earlier details.
project.argument: Defend the ending whose demand is proportionate to the evidence.
project.reflection: Where did an ending promise more than the essay established?

practice.passage: Original fictional conclusion: “One repaired lamp will not solve the waste problem. But a repair service gives residents a usable alternative to disposal. That is a change the council can support this year.”

read.stem: The opening qualification helps the conclusion
options: introduce an unrelated topic.
claim immediate universal success.
propose a limited action without exaggerating its impact.
deny that repair has any value.
rationales: Waste and repair remain central.
The limitation rejects that claim.
The writer distinguishes a practical step from a complete solution.
The following sentences affirm its value.

write.stem: Which final sentence best extends this conclusion?
options: The council should also redesign every road.
Begin with a funded trial and publish what it costs and what residents use.
This will end all waste forever.
The town has considered several waste-reduction programs in recent years.
rationales: The new demand is unsupported.
The action matches the limited, assessable proposal.
The claim exceeds the argument.
The background fact does not advance the proportionate next step developed in the conclusion.

frq.focus: Trace how the final return to the toaster earns a limited but significant conclusion.

concepts.title: Rhetorical analysis
concepts.definition: Rhetorical analysis makes an argument about how a text works. It moves from a precise choice to its function, a plausible audience effect, and the writer’s purpose in context.
concepts.insight: Follow the passage’s movement. A choice may do different work at different moments; explain that progression rather than inventorying devices.
concepts.example: A concession about repair safety makes a recommendation more credible to readers wary of impractical advice.
concepts.misconception: Agreeing with the writer’s position is not the same task as analyzing it.

project.title: The annotated counter-perspective atlas
project.brief: Develop the supplied atlas model into a study of rhetorical choices.
project.composition: Compose three substantial positions on a contested question; choose each style for its audience rather than assigning styles by ideology.
project.visual: Build a triptych whose sequence and visual tensions represent the positions.
project.analysis: Quote and analyze six choices per text, including a choice that could backfire.
project.argument: Defend a position informed by all three perspectives.
project.reflection: How did composing the least familiar perspective alter your analysis of it?

practice.passage: Original fictional essay: “Repair is not always wise. A damaged heater can be dangerous. But treating every broken object as dangerous lets us avoid asking which ones could be safely restored.”

read.stem: The initial concession primarily
options: proves that all repair is unsafe.
ridicules readers for owning heaters.
replaces the argument with technical instructions.
anticipates a legitimate objection before narrowing the argument.
rationales: The final sentence rejects that generalization.
The tone does not ridicule ownership.
No repair procedure is given.
Safety is acknowledged without abandoning repair.

write.stem: Which analytical sentence best explains the choice?
options: I think repair is excellent.
The essay mentions a heater.
By admitting a safety limit, the writer makes the distinction between careful repair and indiscriminate repair more credible.
The writer uses a concession.
rationales: Personal agreement does not analyze rhetoric.
This summarizes a detail without interpretation.
It connects the choice to its argumentative function.
The label alone does not explain its work.

frq.focus: Develop a line of reasoning about choices, not a list of techniques.

concepts.title: Analytical thesis & claims
concepts.definition: An analytical thesis interprets how rhetorical choices contribute to an argument or purpose. It should give the essay something to demonstrate, not merely announce that techniques exist.
concepts.insight: Name functional moves when device labels are unhelpful: reframing a problem, admitting a limit, or inviting a shared judgment.
concepts.example: “Ruiz pairs a repair narrative with practical concessions to make repair seem both possible and responsible” can guide evidence selection.
concepts.misconception: A list of ethos, pathos, and logos is not automatically an interpretation.

project.title: A thesis with consequences
project.brief: Test competing interpretations of the same text.
project.composition: Write two analytical theses about an original speech, then develop the stronger interpretation.
project.visual: Create a claim-and-evidence constellation showing which details each thesis explains.
project.analysis: Account for a passage detail that resists your preferred reading.
project.argument: Defend the interpretation with the greatest explanatory reach.
project.reflection: What did your first thesis make you overlook?

practice.passage: Original fictional passage: “We can honor the past without preserving every inconvenience. Keep the workshop’s shared tools; replace the stairs that prevent some neighbors from entering.”

read.stem: Which interpretation best captures the passage’s reasoning?
options: The writer separates preserving communal value from preserving exclusionary conditions.
The writer rejects every tradition.
The writer values stairs more than access.
The writer considers all change harmful.
rationales: The paired recommendations distinguish what deserves continuity.
Shared tools are explicitly retained.
The proposed replacement indicates the opposite.
A specific change is urged.

write.stem: Which thesis would best guide an analysis?
options: The writer uses contrast and discusses both tradition and change.
The writer explains that the workshop has tools and stairs.
Tradition is good and bad.
By distinguishing shared resources from physical barriers, the writer makes change compatible with honoring the past.
rationales: The statement identifies a technique and topics without interpreting what the contrast accomplishes.
The description names details without interpreting their argumentative relationship.
The general judgment does not analyze the passage.
The claim interprets a choice and its purpose.

frq.focus: Write a thesis that interprets the relationship between practical limits and the call to repair.

concepts.title: Examples & exemplification
concepts.definition: Exemplification develops an idea through cases. A well-chosen case can clarify an abstraction, demonstrate possibility, or challenge a generalization. Its function depends on what the writer asks it to establish.
concepts.insight: Explain the example’s scope. One counterexample can disprove an absolute claim; one successful case rarely proves a universal rule.
concepts.example: A repairable toaster challenges “all broken objects are useless” without proving “all objects should be repaired.”
concepts.misconception: A vivid example is not necessarily representative.

project.title: The exception exhibit
project.brief: Build an argument around a case that resists a familiar rule.
project.composition: Write the strongest version of a general claim, then a response centered on a counterexample.
project.visual: Make an exhibit placing the exceptional case beside typical cases.
project.analysis: Explain what the exception does and does not refute.
project.argument: Revise the original rule so it survives the relevant evidence.
project.reflection: Did the exception destroy the rule or help define its limits?

practice.passage: Original fictional argument: “Not every damaged item requires replacement. A toaster that failed yesterday worked after a bent tab was straightened. Before discarding an object, assess the fault.”

read.stem: The toaster example most directly supports
options: the claim that damage never matters.
the possibility that some faults are repairable.
the claim that all appliances are easy to fix.
the claim that repairs are always free.
rationales: Assessing damage remains necessary.
One repaired case establishes that replacement is not always necessary.
The example cannot establish a universal rule.
No cost claim is made.

write.stem: Which addition best prevents overgeneralization?
options: Other faults may make repair unsafe or uneconomical, so inspection remains essential.
This single toaster proves every repair will succeed.
All repairers have identical skills.
Some residents prefer newer designs even when an old object still works.
rationales: The limit keeps the example’s scope proportionate.
This exceeds the evidence.
The unsupported claim does not follow.
Preference for replacement is distinct from whether a damaged object can be responsibly repaired.

frq.focus: Explain how the contrasting toaster and heater examples develop a bounded recommendation.

concepts.title: Classification & arrangement
concepts.definition: Classification groups cases by a chosen principle. Categories can reveal patterns and guide decisions, but they may also conceal overlap or create a false binary.
concepts.insight: Name the organizing principle and test borderline cases. Ask whether categories are useful for this purpose rather than naturally fixed.
concepts.example: Sorting repairs by safety and cost is more useful for a repair decision than sorting by color.
concepts.misconception: Categories are analytical choices, not automatically objective divisions.

project.title: The cabinet that will not close
project.brief: Design a classification system and confront its difficult cases.
project.composition: Write a guide classifying public resources by need, access, or cost, plus a critique of your own system.
project.visual: Build a cabinet with movable labels and an explicit overlap drawer.
project.analysis: Analyze who or what disappears under each category.
project.argument: Defend a revised classification suited to a concrete decision.
project.reflection: Which borderline case exposed a weakness in your organizing principle?

practice.passage: Original fictional guide: “Sort objects into those safe to repair at home, those requiring a specialist, and those whose risks outweigh repair benefits. Price alone cannot make this decision.”

read.stem: The classification is primarily organized by
options: the owners’ ages.
the assumption that cheap objects are worthless.
the conditions under which repair is responsible.
the objects’ decorative appearance.
rationales: Owner age is not mentioned.
The passage rejects price as the only basis.
Safety and expertise determine the groups.
Appearance is not used.

write.stem: Which addition would best clarify a category boundary?
options: The guide has three categories.
An exposed electrical fault belongs with a qualified specialist, even in an inexpensive object.
Red objects belong together.
Every object fits equally well everywhere.
rationales: Counting categories does not explain their boundaries.
The case illustrates how expertise matters more than price.
Color changes the organizing principle without purpose.
This erases useful distinctions.

frq.focus: Analyze the distinctions Ruiz draws among kinds of objects, choices, and repair conditions.

concepts.title: Visual rhetoric
concepts.definition: Images, layout, scale, typography, and sequence can make claims or direct attention. Analyze visual choices in their situation and explain how they frame relationships, values, or evidence.
concepts.insight: Distinguish what is visible from what you infer. Consider what the frame excludes and whether the visual distorts a quantitative relationship.
concepts.example: A small person beside an oversized locked door can emphasize unequal power, but the interpretation depends on context.
concepts.misconception: Naming colors without explaining their function is not visual analysis.

project.title: Two posters, one policy
project.brief: Make the same proposal visible from competing perspectives.
project.composition: Write two position statements on a public-space redesign and concise text for their posters.
project.visual: Create contrasting posters using scale, placement, and negative space deliberately; supply text descriptions.
project.analysis: Analyze how each poster guides attention and what it leaves outside the frame.
project.argument: Defend the more responsible visual argument using explicit criteria.
project.reflection: Which visual choice persuaded efficiently but oversimplified the issue?

practice.passage: Original fictional poster description: A small figure waits outside an oversized library door. The posted hours end at 6 p.m.; the figure’s work badge reads “Shift ends 6 p.m.” The caption asks for an evening-hours trial.

read.stem: The contrast in scale primarily emphasizes
options: the architectural dimensions of an actual building.
the worker’s dislike of books.
the certainty that every worker has this schedule.
the individual’s difficulty accessing an institution.
rationales: The stylized description supplies no measurements.
The figure waits to enter.
One visual case cannot establish universal schedules.
The large barrier and incompatible times frame exclusion.

write.stem: Which addition would best support the poster’s proposal without overstating its evidence?
options: A photograph of the library’s newest collection of books.
A fabricated attendance total presented as measured.
A small box explaining the trial’s hours, cost, and review date.
A claim that every resident is excluded.
rationales: The collection may illustrate value, but it does not specify how the proposed evening trial would work.
Invented evidence would mislead readers.
Specific conditions connect the image to a feasible request.
The universal claim exceeds the image.

frq.focus: Analyze how descriptions of exhibit placement make an argument about whose history is visible.

concepts.title: Close reading & inference
concepts.definition: Close reading builds an interpretation from specific textual relationships: wording, sequence, emphasis, and what a passage leaves unresolved. An inference moves beyond what is directly stated while remaining accountable to those details.
concepts.insight: Separate observation, inference, and speculation. Test your interpretation against a detail that could challenge it. Explain the path from language to meaning rather than replacing evidence with a description of the writer’s intentions.
concepts.example: If a speaker repeats “for now” while endorsing a policy, the phrase may qualify the endorsement. A claim of secret hostility would require additional evidence.
concepts.misconception: A possible interpretation is not necessarily a well-supported one. Close reading does not give every interpretation equal evidentiary weight.

project.title: The annotation hearing
project.brief: Put two plausible readings of one passage on trial.
project.composition: Choose a short public-domain text or use an original passage in this library. Write two 400-word interpretations that make different claims about the same choice, quoting precise details. Keep an observation log separate from your inferences.
project.visual: Create a transparent overlay or two-column evidence map showing which details support both readings and which distinguish them. Provide a sequential text version.
project.analysis: Explain six annotation decisions, including one omission. Identify how selection or arrangement makes one interpretation appear stronger.
project.argument: Defend the better-supported reading while preserving a real ambiguity. Answer the rival reading’s strongest evidence, then revise one inference after a reader traces it back to the passage.
project.reflection: Which interpretation changed when you stopped treating a plausible motive as a textual fact?

practice.passage: Original fictional speech excerpt: “We will keep the Saturday workshop, for now. The sign-up sheet records enthusiasm, but a signature cannot tell us whether someone can afford the bus fare. Before we call the empty chairs a lack of interest, let us ask who could reach the room. After that inquiry, we can decide whether to change the workshop or the route to it.”

read.stem: Which interpretation of the speaker’s position is best supported by the passage?
options: The speaker intends to cancel the workshop regardless of the inquiry’s findings.
The speaker supports continuing the workshop provisionally while investigating an alternative explanation for low attendance.
The speaker believes sign-up sheets have no value in planning a workshop.
The speaker has established that bus fares are the sole cause of empty chairs.
rationales: The final sentence leaves the decision open to the inquiry’s results.
“For now” limits the commitment, and the fare question introduces an access explanation.
The passage limits what signatures establish without rejecting every use of them.
The speaker proposes an inquiry rather than announcing a proven cause.

write.stem: A student argues that the speaker delays judgment to improve the decision. Which commentary best explains evidence for that claim?
options: By distinguishing willingness to sign up from ability to arrive, the speaker shows why attendance alone cannot yet justify cancellation.
The speaker uses the words “sign-up sheet,” which makes the speech concrete.
The speaker probably disliked the original workshop organizers.
The passage contains a discussion of transportation and workshops.
rationales: This connects two textual details to the reasoning behind delaying the decision.
This observation does not explain how the detail supports the claim about judgment.
The speculation about motive is unsupported by the passage.
This summarizes the topic without explaining the argumentative relationship.

frq.focus: Test your interpretation of the speaker’s attitude against both the acknowledgment of staff effort and the criticism of the notice.

concepts.title: Rhetorical shifts
concepts.definition: A rhetorical shift changes a text’s strategy, focus, tone, scale, or relationship to its audience. Its importance lies in how the movement changes the argument’s work, not simply in where a new paragraph begins.
concepts.insight: Describe the movement with two precise terms: from a personal observation to a public criterion, or from concession to a bounded proposal. Locate a verbal or structural cue and explain why the new move follows the earlier one.
concepts.example: A writer may begin with an admired family object, then shift to the labor required to repair it, turning nostalgia into an argument about practical responsibility.
concepts.misconception: A transition word can signal a shift, but it does not explain the shift’s function. Some consequential shifts occur without an explicit transition.

project.title: The hinge exhibition
project.brief: Make the turning point of an argument visible and test an alternative order.
project.composition: Write a 600-word public address that moves from a personal scene to an institutional proposal. Produce a second version with the same evidence but a different turning point. Label fictional scenes.
project.visual: Build a hinged poster or a sequence of panels that physically turns at the argumentative shift. Include a text version explaining the sequence and the hinge.
project.analysis: Quote the sentences before and after each turning point. Analyze six choices that prepare readers for, or resist, the change in scale and purpose.
project.argument: Defend one version’s sequence for a named audience. Explain what the alternative version makes easier to understand, then revise the weaker transition after a reader outlines both versions.
project.reflection: Did your shift change the argument’s reasoning or only announce a new topic?

practice.passage: Original fictional essay excerpt: “My grandfather’s repaired kettle sat in the kitchen for thirty years. Its mismatched handle made it look less like a product than a history. Yet affection cannot hold a handle in place. Someone had to know which screw would fit, and somewhere had to sell it. If we want repair to become ordinary again, we must discuss parts and training as well as memories.”

read.stem: The sentence “Yet affection cannot hold a handle in place” marks a shift from
options: a criticism of the grandfather to praise for commercial manufacturers.
a comparison of repair techniques to an unrelated family anecdote.
an account of an object’s emotional significance to the practical conditions that make repair possible.
a defense of repair to a recommendation that old objects be replaced.
rationales: Neither criticism of the grandfather nor praise for manufacturers appears.
The family anecdote comes first and remains connected to the argument.
The next sentences identify skills and parts, turning memory toward material requirements.
The passage continues to support repair while explaining its requirements.

write.stem: The writer wants a final sentence that connects the personal example to a public proposal. Which choice best achieves that goal?
options: Training matters, and another subject worth considering is the design of modern kitchens.
A town repair program should therefore fund access to parts and instruction, giving more families the means to keep valued objects in use.
My grandfather’s kettle was blue, with a dark patch near the spout.
Many people remember objects from their childhood kitchens.
rationales: This introduces a new topic instead of completing the existing movement.
The sentence links practical conditions to a proposal while retaining the example’s personal stakes.
The detail returns to description without advancing the public proposal.
The generalization extends nostalgia but does not connect it to action.

frq.focus: Explain how movements between remembered objects, practical obstacles, and public responsibilities develop the essay’s argument.

concepts.title: Argument organization
concepts.definition: Organization is the strategic placement of claims, evidence, qualifications, and responses. Different arrangements can produce different expectations and make reasoning easier or harder to follow.
concepts.insight: Choose an order for the audience’s questions: what is happening, why it matters, what alternatives exist, and what follows.
concepts.example: A skeptical audience may need an objection addressed before it will consider a proposal.
concepts.misconception: A five-paragraph structure is an option, not an AP requirement.

project.title: The reversible editorial
project.brief: Test whether a different order changes an argument’s force.
project.composition: Write an editorial and a second version using the same evidence in a substantially different order.
project.visual: Create a folding sequence that can be read in either direction.
project.analysis: Compare where readers encounter stakes, objections, and conclusions.
project.argument: Defend the arrangement that best supports your reasoning.
project.reflection: What did the alternate order reveal about a weak transition or assumption?

practice.passage: Original fictional outline: Explain a missing service; establish who needs it; compare possible responses; recommend a limited trial.

read.stem: The arrangement supports the recommendation by
options: establishing need and evaluating alternatives before proposing action.
withholding the problem until the end.
treating every alternative as equally useful without comparison.
placing the conclusion before any context.
rationales: The sequence gives readers grounds for the recommendation.
The problem comes first.
Comparison is an explicit step.
The recommendation comes last.

write.stem: For readers who believe the service already exists, which addition should come early?
options: A narrative about the writer’s first positive experience with the existing service.
A repeated demand for immediate approval.
A list of decorative design choices.
A distinction between the existing service and the unmet need.
rationales: The experience might establish interest but does not distinguish the existing service from the unmet need.
Repetition leaves the misunderstanding intact.
Decoration does not establish need.
The audience must understand the gap before evaluating responses.

frq.focus: Trace why the address moves from objects to missing lives, then to collection practices.

concepts.title: Unity & coherence
concepts.definition: Unity means the parts serve a governing purpose. Coherence means readers can follow their relationships. A paragraph may stay on one topic yet remain incoherent if the links among its claims are unclear.
concepts.insight: Track referents, repeated concepts, and the movement from known information to new information. Repair missing reasoning before adding transition words.
concepts.example: “That barrier” can connect a proposed remedy to an access problem already explained.
concepts.misconception: Sentences about the same topic do not necessarily form a connected argument.

project.title: A guided exhibit
project.brief: Arrange information so a visitor can reconstruct the argument.
project.composition: Write an exhibit script and an intentionally scrambled version for comparison.
project.visual: Build a path of panels with explicit conceptual handoffs.
project.analysis: Explain where a visitor needs a reference, definition, or inference.
project.argument: Defend the revisions that most improve understanding.
project.reflection: Which confusion came from missing logic rather than missing transition words?

practice.passage: Original fictional draft: “The archive accepts family photographs. These contributions reveal daily routines. Those routines help explain how official policies affected ordinary lives.”

read.stem: The paragraph’s coherence depends chiefly on
options: avoiding all references to earlier ideas.
carrying a concept from each sentence into the next.
repeating the same full sentence.
introducing unrelated facts at each step.
rationales: The paragraph uses explicit references.
Photographs become contributions, then routines become the next subject.
No sentence is repeated.
Each sentence develops the previous one.

write.stem: Which sentence would best continue the line of reasoning?
options: For that reason, personal collections can complement the town’s official records.
The archive recently purchased additional photograph sleeves.
Visitors can consult the archive during its posted opening hours.
Official policy records should therefore replace all personal contributions.
rationales: The conclusion follows from the relationship just explained.
Storage equipment is relevant to archives but does not extend the claim about everyday experience and policy.
Availability introduces logistics rather than developing the value of personal records.
The conclusion reverses the paragraph’s reasoning about the complementary value of personal material.

frq.focus: Explain how recurring objects and terms connect the address’s stages.

concepts.title: Transitions & logical relationships
concepts.definition: Transitions signal relationships such as contrast, consequence, extension, and concession. They include repeated concepts and carefully placed phrases, not just a stock list of linking words.
concepts.insight: Name the actual relationship before choosing a transition. A word such as “therefore” cannot create a causal connection the reasoning has not earned.
concepts.example: “That benefit has a cost” both refers backward and introduces a tension.
concepts.misconception: Adding “furthermore” to every paragraph does not establish progression.

project.title: The connective-tissue zine
project.brief: Make the relationships between claims visible.
project.composition: Write a multi-section argument and a revision that changes three logical relationships.
project.visual: Design a zine whose folds represent contrast, extension, and consequence.
project.analysis: Explain how each revised transition changes what a reader can infer.
project.argument: Defend the sequence that accurately represents the evidence.
project.reflection: Where did a familiar transition conceal a logical gap?

practice.passage: Original fictional draft: “Digital copies make records easier to search. ___, they do not preserve the texture, size, or wear of an original object.”

read.stem: The relationship between the sentences is one of
options: two identical claims.
unrelated historical events.
benefit followed by limitation.
cause followed by an inevitable result.
rationales: The sentences concern different capacities.
Both concern records and representation.
Searchability is acknowledged before an omitted dimension is identified.
Searchability does not cause loss of texture.

write.stem: Which transition best expresses this relationship?
options: Similarly
However
Consequently
For example
rationales: The relationship is contrast, not similarity.
It signals the limit on the preceding benefit.
It incorrectly implies a causal result.
The second sentence is not an example of easier searching.

frq.focus: Examine transitions that distinguish memory from certainty and participation from extraction.

concepts.title: Diction & register
concepts.definition: Diction is word choice; register is the level and kind of language appropriate to a social situation. Concrete verbs, specialized terms, and everyday language can all be effective when they serve a purpose.
concepts.insight: Discuss a precise word in context and compare a plausible alternative. Explain the difference in emphasis, relationship, or judgment.
concepts.example: Calling a collection “evidence” rather than “treasure” changes what readers are invited to do with it.
concepts.misconception: Long words are not inherently more sophisticated.

project.title: The word-choice print shop
project.brief: Explore how a few words change a public message.
project.composition: Write two versions of a public appeal with different registers for defined audiences.
project.visual: Create paired broadsides that emphasize the changed words.
project.analysis: Analyze six substitutions and their effects on precision and relationship.
project.argument: Defend which choices inform readers and which risk manipulating them.
project.reflection: Which simpler word made your reasoning more precise?

practice.passage: Original fictional address: “The archive does not merely store objects; it safeguards traces of lives.”

read.stem: Compared with “stores,” “safeguards” emphasizes
options: the efficiency of organizing material for retrieval.
indifference toward the collection.
the commercial price of every object.
a responsibility to protect vulnerable material.
rationales: Efficient organization is compatible with safeguarding, but the word’s distinguishing implication is protection.
Safeguarding implies care.
Price is not specified.
The verb gives preservation an ethical dimension.

write.stem: For a practical instruction to volunteers, which wording is clearest?
options: Do something nice with the pictures.
Photos are very meaningful.
Place each photograph in a labeled protective sleeve.
Enact archival transcendence upon the visual artifact.
rationales: The vague request lacks a procedure.
The statement does not instruct.
Concrete action and object make the task usable.
The abstraction obscures the task.

frq.focus: Analyze how words about care and absence develop the archive’s responsibilities.

concepts.title: Connotation & framing
concepts.definition: Connotation is the association or evaluative coloring a word carries beyond its basic reference. Framing selects a lens through which readers interpret an issue.
concepts.insight: Compare labels for the same referent and ask which judgment each encourages. Avoid assuming connotations are identical for every audience.
concepts.example: “Unused space” and “a place kept open” can describe the same area while implying opposite judgments.
concepts.misconception: A negative-sounding word does not prove the writer’s entire tone is hostile.

project.title: The label swap
project.brief: Reveal how naming can make a policy seem natural or objectionable.
project.composition: Write two short policy briefs that use competing labels for the same change, then a transparent revision.
project.visual: Design removable labels over one shared diagram.
project.analysis: Explain how each label activates assumptions before evidence appears.
project.argument: Defend a label that is both useful and fair.
project.reflection: Which label made an unsupported conclusion feel settled?

practice.passage: Original fictional debate: One speaker calls a proposed archive “a warehouse of clutter”; another calls it “a record of everyday lives.”

read.stem: The competing phrases chiefly differ in how they
options: assign value to the same collection.
state the building’s precise capacity.
identify different opening hours.
prove either position correct.
rationales: Clutter dismisses what a record treats as meaningful.
Neither gives dimensions.
Hours are not mentioned.
Labels frame judgment but do not establish evidence.

write.stem: Which revision best reduces loaded framing while retaining the issue?
options: The worthless junk must be saved.
Only foolish people question the archive.
The collection is unquestionably perfect.
The proposal would preserve household objects as historical records; its value and cost need evaluation.
rationales: The phrase remains loaded and internally strained.
The insult forecloses evaluation.
The absolute praise avoids analysis.
It identifies the action and leaves judgment open to evidence.

frq.focus: Explain how contrasting labels influence what counts as historically significant.

concepts.title: Tone & tonal shifts
concepts.definition: Tone is the attitude a text conveys toward its subject or audience. It emerges from diction, syntax, detail, and stance, and it may shift as the writer’s purpose develops.
concepts.insight: Support a tone claim with specific language. A paired description such as “respectful but insistent” can capture a tension that a single adjective misses.
concepts.example: Acknowledging a council’s duty before challenging its measure of value creates a respectful yet critical stance.
concepts.misconception: Tone is not simply the emotion a reader happens to feel.

project.title: The tonal weather map
project.brief: Trace a purposeful change in attitude.
project.composition: Write an address that moves through three justified tones without changing its central position.
project.visual: Create a weather map showing the textual boundaries and causes of the shifts.
project.analysis: Analyze the words and sentence patterns that make each transition perceptible.
project.argument: Defend whether each shift serves the audience or merely adds drama.
project.reflection: Where did your intended tone differ from a reader’s interpretation?

practice.passage: Original fictional address: “We are grateful for the records donated so far. Yet gratitude must not keep us from asking whose lives remain absent.”

read.stem: The tone is best described as
options: triumphant about a completed collection.
appreciative but searching.
wholly dismissive of donors.
indifferent to the archive’s limits.
rationales: The collection remains incomplete.
Thanks coexist with a critical question about omission.
The opening expresses gratitude.
The second sentence presses that concern.

write.stem: Which sentence preserves that tone?
options: Your gifts made this work possible; further contributions can help us see what we have missed.
The collection is useless.
We have nothing left to learn.
Donors should be ashamed of everything.
rationales: It combines appreciation with continued inquiry.
This abandons appreciation.
This abandons inquiry.
This replaces measured critique with accusation.

frq.focus: Trace shifts between appreciation, self-critique, caution, and invitation.

concepts.title: Syntax & rhetorical effect
concepts.definition: Syntax is the arrangement of words, phrases, and clauses. Length, repetition, subordination, and placement can manage pace and establish relationships among ideas.
concepts.insight: Describe what the structure does in this sentence. A short sentence can clarify, interrupt, or emphasize; its effect is not fixed by its length.
concepts.example: After a long account of missing records, “We do not know” can make uncertainty unmistakable.
concepts.misconception: Long sentences are not always complex in thought, and short ones are not always simple.

project.title: The sentence score
project.brief: Treat a paragraph’s syntax as a sequence of deliberate decisions.
project.composition: Write two versions of an argument: one built around accumulation and one around interruption.
project.visual: Score the sentences as visual measures showing clauses, pauses, and emphasis.
project.analysis: Explain where structure changes the relation between claims.
project.argument: Defend the version that makes the reasoning clearer for its audience.
project.reflection: Which rhythmic choice interfered with the meaning you intended?

practice.passage: Original fictional address: “We know the factory’s opening date, the architect’s name, and the owner’s address. We do not know where its workers ate.”

read.stem: The contrast in sentence structure primarily
options: shows that workers never ate.
makes the two kinds of knowledge indistinguishable.
makes an absence of everyday history stand out against accumulated official detail.
proves that official records are inaccurate.
rationales: The speaker states missing knowledge, not absence of meals.
The structure emphasizes their difference.
The shorter second sentence interrupts a list of documented facts.
The facts may be accurate but incomplete.

write.stem: Which revision best preserves this emphasis?
options: Everything about the workers is known.
Official facts fill our files. The workers’ routines remain missing.
We know some things and maybe other things too.
Records, records, records.
rationales: This reverses the meaning.
The compact contrast keeps the unequal record visible.
The vague wording erases the distinction.
Repetition alone does not express the relationship.

frq.focus: Connect syntactic contrasts and accumulations to Bell’s argument about historical visibility.

concepts.title: Cumulative & periodic sentences
concepts.definition: A cumulative sentence presents a main clause and then adds modifying detail. A periodic sentence delays its main clause or grammatical completion until after preparatory material. The placement changes how a reader encounters the relationship among ideas.
concepts.insight: Mark the main clause before naming the pattern. Then explain what the reader learns immediately and what must be held in suspense. Neither pattern has an automatic emotional effect; context determines whether delay feels clarifying, solemn, or cumbersome.
concepts.example: “We opened the hall, carrying chairs from three classrooms” gives the action first. “After the chairs arrived and the doors were cleared, we opened the hall” prepares conditions before the action.
concepts.misconception: A long sentence is not necessarily periodic, and a short sentence can still delay its main clause. Length and grammatical arrangement are different features.

project.title: The opening-night reveal
project.brief: Compose two versions of a public message with different patterns of arrival.
project.composition: Write a 500-word opening address for a community exhibition. Revise six sentences into paired cumulative and periodic forms while preserving their claims. Produce a second version incorporating your strongest alternatives.
project.visual: Build a miniature paper stage or a flat reveal sequence. Place the main clause before or behind movable panels containing its modifiers, so readers encounter each sentence in order. Include full sentence text and explain how the reveal changes emphasis.
project.analysis: Analyze all six pairs in context. Explain where delaying the main clause changes emphasis or increases memory demands; avoid assigning a fixed effect to a pattern.
project.argument: Defend which version better serves listeners hearing the message once. Test it aloud or with a peer, then revise two sentences based on what listeners can reconstruct.
project.reflection: Where did a sentence that looked impressive on the page make the relationship among ideas harder to hear?

practice.passage: Original fictional opening address: “After the volunteers carried the tables upstairs, after the neighbors brought photographs from drawers and wallets, after the oldest resident found a chair near the window, the exhibition finally opened. The room filled slowly, with stories crossing the spaces between display cases. What looked like a collection of objects became a gathering of people able to explain them.”

read.stem: The arrangement of the first sentence chiefly emphasizes
options: the opening as an immediate fact followed by optional background details.
a conflict between volunteers and residents over who owns the objects.
the inability of chronological sequence to explain the event.
the collective preparations that precede the opening by withholding the main event until the end.
rationales: The main event is delayed rather than stated first.
The sentence describes coordinated preparation, not a dispute.
The sequence helps establish the preparations on which the opening depends.
The repeated introductory clauses delay “the exhibition finally opened” and foreground its enabling work.

write.stem: The writer wants to state the main event first and then accumulate details of participation. Which revision best accomplishes this goal?
options: Although the exhibition finally opened, the oldest visitor sat near the window.
Volunteers carried tables upstairs because the exhibition had already opened.
The exhibition finally opened, its tables carried upstairs by volunteers, its photographs brought by neighbors, its oldest visitor seated near the window.
After the tables and photographs arrived, the exhibition finally opened.
rationales: This creates a concessive relationship not supported by the original.
This reverses the timing and changes the causal relationship.
The main clause arrives first, followed by details modifying the event.
The main clause remains delayed and much of the participation is removed.

frq.focus: Examine how the ordering of clauses controls what the audience must consider before accepting the speaker’s proposal.

concepts.title: Cohesion & reference
concepts.definition: Cohesion connects sentences through recurring terms, pronouns, demonstratives, and other explicit links. Reference is clear when a reader can identify what an expression such as “they” or “this change” points to.
concepts.insight: Trace each reference to a specific noun or idea. A summary noun can carry reasoning forward: “this delay” names a consequence, while “this disagreement” names a relationship. Repetition can provide precision when synonyms would blur the subject.
concepts.example: After describing an office that closes before workers arrive, “this scheduling barrier” identifies the problem more clearly than an isolated “this.”
concepts.misconception: Clear reference helps readers follow an argument but cannot make disconnected claims logically coherent. A pronoun may be grammatically possible and still be ambiguous.

project.title: The trail of this
project.brief: Build and repair a reader’s path through a complex explanation.
project.composition: Write a 500-word explanation of a school process involving at least three groups. Create a second version that improves unclear references without simplifying away important relationships. Preserve both drafts.
project.visual: Map nouns and referring expressions as a trail with labeled branches. Distinguish deliberate repetition from ambiguity; provide a sentence-by-sentence text equivalent.
project.analysis: Analyze six revisions, explaining not only what each expression refers to but what interpretation the earlier wording invited.
project.argument: Defend a principle for balancing concision with explicit repetition. Test two ambiguous sentences with readers and revise them using the responses as limited evidence.
project.reflection: When did replacing a repeated noun with a more elegant phrase make the argument less precise?

practice.passage: Original fictional report: “The student editors asked the librarians to extend the archive’s opening hours. They said the current schedule prevented research after class. The librarians proposed a two-week trial with volunteers. This would give the editors time to gather evidence about demand before requesting a permanent change.” The writer intends the second sentence to report the editors’ concern.

read.stem: Why might the pronoun “They” in the second sentence impede understanding?
options: Both the editors and the librarians are plausible plural referents, so the source of the concern is uncertain.
The pronoun disagrees in number with every noun in the preceding sentence.
The pronoun establishes that the librarians rejected the request.
The pronoun makes the description shift from past to future tense.
rationales: The previous sentence supplies two groups, and the pronoun does not specify which spoke.
Both “editors” and “librarians” are plural.
It does not establish rejection; its referent is ambiguous.
The tense remains past in “said” and “prevented.”

write.stem: Which revision of the second sentence most clearly expresses the writer’s intended meaning?
options: They explained to them that the current schedule prevented research after class.
The librarians explained that the editors preferred researching during class.
This prevented research after class, as they said.
The editors explained that the current schedule prevented their research after class.
rationales: The two pronouns preserve or increase uncertainty about the groups.
The revision changes both the speaker and the substance of the concern.
Both the cause and the source remain unclear.
The revision names the intended speakers and ties the consequence to their work.

frq.prompt: Writers are often encouraged to avoid repeating words, yet repetition can preserve precision. Write an essay that argues your position on when clarity should take precedence over stylistic variety.
frq.focus: Use examples in which a wording choice affects what a reader can understand or do.

concepts.title: Synthesis as argument
concepts.definition: Synthesis uses relationships among sources to develop your own position. Sources can agree, qualify, complicate, or contradict one another; your reasoning decides what the relationship means.
concepts.insight: Organize around claims rather than one paragraph per source. Explain what becomes visible when two sources are read together.
concepts.example: A planning memo and a shop owner’s letter can jointly support a trial that protects access while testing a redesign.
concepts.misconception: Citing several sources is not sufficient if they remain isolated summaries.

project.title: The source-conversation atlas
project.brief: Build a position from sources that do different kinds of work.
project.composition: Write a sourced recommendation and an informed dissent using at least four traceable sources.
project.visual: Create a map whose edges name agreements, qualifications, and tensions.
project.analysis: Explain how source relationships changed two major claims.
project.argument: Defend a qualified recommendation that preserves a real objection.
project.reflection: Which source changed the question you thought you were answering?

practice.passage: Original fictional sources: A planning memo predicts increased use after adding seating. A shop owner supports seating if loading access remains. A student group asks for free places to gather.

read.stem: Which claim best synthesizes the sources?
options: Every source opposes seating.
Only shop owners have relevant concerns.
A memo, a letter, and a statement exist.
A redesign could expand gathering space if it preserves necessary access.
rationales: All three allow or support it.
This discards the other perspectives without reasoning.
This catalogs sources instead of synthesizing them.
The claim combines the benefit with the stakeholder’s condition.

write.stem: Which organization best supports synthesis?
options: Quote only the longest source.
Use sources only in the final sentence.
Group sources by access, benefits, and implementation questions.
Summarize each source without making a claim.
rationales: Length is not a criterion for relevance.
Late citation cannot substitute for developed reasoning.
Issue-based groups let sources interact within claims.
Summary alone leaves the argument undeveloped.

frq.prompt: Develop a position on whether Bellweather should redesign its public square.
frq.focus: Use relationships among sources to develop your own criteria.

concepts.title: Source credibility & perspective
concepts.definition: Evaluate a source’s relevant expertise, evidence, method, proximity, purpose, and limits. A stakeholder’s interest can shape a perspective without making all of its observations false.
concepts.insight: Match the source to the claim it can support. Distinguish reliable testimony about an experience from authority over a whole population.
concepts.example: A shop owner can describe delivery problems but cannot establish townwide travel patterns without broader evidence.
concepts.misconception: Bias is a reason to investigate a claim, not a shortcut for dismissing it.

project.title: The source hearing
project.brief: Assign sources roles based on what they can actually establish.
project.composition: Write an evidence brief and a cross-examination of its strongest source.
project.visual: Design source identity cards showing expertise, method, interest, and limits.
project.analysis: Explain which claims each source can support and where corroboration is needed.
project.argument: Defend which source deserves the most weight for one specific decision.
project.reflection: Did apparent authority distract you from a weak method?

practice.passage: Original fictional letter: “I own a shop beside the square. Deliveries already compete for space. I have not counted how customers travel, but I worry that losing parking will affect them.”

read.stem: The source is strongest as evidence of
options: the owner’s observed delivery concerns.
the exact proportion of customers who drive.
the inevitable failure of any redesign.
all residents’ preferences.
rationales: The writer has direct experience with that issue.
The writer explicitly has not counted it.
The letter raises concerns rather than proving failure.
One stakeholder cannot represent everyone.

write.stem: Which sentence uses this source responsibly?
options: The letter proves every customer drives.
The owner has an interest, so every observation is false.
The letter supplies a complete traffic study.
The owner’s account identifies a loading issue that the trial should investigate.
rationales: The claim contradicts the source’s uncertainty.
Interest does not invalidate all testimony.
No such study is described.
It uses the testimony within its stated limits.

frq.prompt: Develop a position on what evidence should carry the greatest weight in Bellweather’s decision about its public square.
frq.focus: Evaluate sources in relation to particular claims, not by reputation alone.

concepts.title: Agreement, tension & source dialogue
concepts.definition: Sources can address different aspects of a question without directly disagreeing. Productive dialogue identifies the precise point of overlap or tension and uses it to refine a claim.
concepts.insight: Ask whether sources use the same definition, population, period, or criterion. Apparent contradictions may disappear when scope becomes clear.
concepts.example: A planner’s interest in pedestrian space and an access group’s request for nearby parking can coexist in one design.
concepts.misconception: Different recommendations do not always reflect incompatible values.

project.title: A roundtable in six voices
project.brief: Stage a source-based deliberation with a real unresolved tension.
project.composition: Write a dialogue among four sourced perspectives and a moderator’s reasoned recommendation.
project.visual: Create a circular seating diagram with labeled areas of agreement.
project.analysis: Analyze where perspectives address different questions or challenge the same claim.
project.argument: Defend a resolution that does not pretend all interests are satisfied.
project.reflection: Which apparent contradiction became a difference in scope?

practice.passage: Original fictional statements: “Create a continuous pedestrian route,” says the planning office. “Retain nearby accessible parking and maintain the route,” says the access group.

read.stem: The statements are best understood as
options: irrelevant to the same proposal.
potentially compatible requirements for a more usable space.
proof that accessibility and walking are opposites.
identical recommendations in every detail.
rationales: Both address use of the square.
A route and accessible parking can coexist.
The statements do not establish that opposition.
The access group adds parking and maintenance requirements.

write.stem: Which synthesis sentence most accurately represents their relationship?
options: The access group extends the planning office’s emphasis on routes by specifying parking and maintenance conditions.
The access group rejects all pedestrian access.
Both groups demand removal of every parking space.
The two sources cannot be compared.
rationales: It identifies agreement and added requirements.
This misrepresents its position.
Neither statement says this.
They share a relevant subject and criteria.

frq.prompt: Develop a position on how Bellweather should balance competing definitions of access in redesigning its square.
frq.focus: Distinguish a genuine conflict from compatible conditions.

concepts.title: Quotation, paraphrase & integration
concepts.definition: Use a quotation when exact wording matters; paraphrase when the idea matters more than its phrasing. Introduce the material, identify its source, and explain its contribution to your claim.
concepts.insight: Preserve qualifiers and context. A paraphrase changes language and structure while maintaining meaning; swapping a few words is not enough.
concepts.example: “May increase use” cannot responsibly become “will guarantee success.”
concepts.misconception: A quotation does not explain its own relevance.

project.title: The quotation loom
project.brief: Weave distinct source voices into a coherent argument.
project.composition: Write a synthesis paragraph using quotation, another using paraphrase, then a full revised recommendation.
project.visual: Design a woven strip whose colors distinguish source material from your reasoning.
project.analysis: Explain where exact language is necessary and where paraphrase improves clarity.
project.argument: Defend a revision that preserves the source’s limits.
project.reflection: Where did integrating a source change your own claim?

practice.passage: Original fictional memo: “The pilot may reveal circulation problems, but it cannot reproduce the shade of mature trees.”

read.stem: Which paraphrase best preserves the memo’s meaning?
options: The trial can simulate every feature of the final design.
The trial has no informational value.
The trial can help assess movement but cannot fully test future shade.
The trial will prove that trees are unnecessary.
rationales: The source explicitly denies this.
The memo identifies circulation information.
Both potential value and limitation remain.
The source makes no such claim.

write.stem: Which sentence best integrates the memo into an argument?
options: The trial guarantees success (Source A).
Because the trial cannot simulate mature shade, the council should treat its results as partial evidence rather than a complete test (Source A).
“Mature trees.”
Source A is a source that says things.
rationales: A citation cannot make a misrepresentation accurate.
The sentence identifies the source and explains its implication.
The fragment gives no context or reasoning.
This provides neither substance nor analysis.

frq.prompt: Develop a position on the role a temporary trial should play in Bellweather’s redesign decision.
frq.focus: Integrate sources accurately, including their qualifications.

concepts.title: Quantitative & visual evidence
concepts.definition: Numbers require a denominator, measurement method, period, and appropriate comparison. A chart’s scale and categories can influence interpretation even when its plotted values are accurate.
concepts.insight: Distinguish counts from rates and association from causation. State what was measured before interpreting what it means.
concepts.example: 104 long visits out of 260 is 40%; 42 out of 180 is about 23%. Different totals matter to the comparison.
concepts.misconception: A larger number does not by itself explain why a change occurred.

project.title: The honest data poster
project.brief: Present the same data clearly and then expose a misleading version.
project.composition: Write a quantitative argument and a critique of an exaggerated presentation.
project.visual: Create two charts with labeled scales, units, denominators, and text equivalents.
project.analysis: Explain how scale and sampling alter what readers can infer.
project.argument: Defend a conclusion that the data actually support.
project.reflection: Which visually impressive claim disappeared when you included the denominator?

practice.passage: Original simulated observations: Existing layout: 180 visits, 42 lasting at least 15 minutes. Temporary seating: 260 visits, 104 lasting at least 15 minutes. Each condition was observed on two Saturdays; visitors were not randomly assigned.

read.stem: Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Seating alone certainly caused the increase.
Every visitor stayed longer.
The pilot establishes annual use.
The observed proportion of longer visits was greater with temporary seating.
rationales: The observational design does not isolate causation.
The table reports groups, not changes for every person.
Four Saturdays cannot establish the entire year.
104/260 is 40%, compared with 42/180, about 23%.

write.stem: Which sentence most responsibly uses these data?
options: The sample proves all residents support construction.
There is no difference between the recorded proportions.
The observations suggest promise, but more varied sessions are needed to assess typical use.
The redesign will double every form of participation.
rationales: Visits are not a representative opinion survey.
The supplied counts show a difference.
The inference acknowledges the limited sampling.
The claim exceeds the measured outcome.

frq.prompt: Develop a position on the extent to which Bellweather’s pilot data justify a permanent redesign.
frq.focus: Explain denominators, sampling limits, and what other sources contribute.

concepts.title: Analogy, metaphor & imagery
concepts.definition: An analogy reasons from a relevant similarity; a metaphor presents one thing in terms of another. Imagery makes an experience perceptible. These choices can clarify unfamiliar ideas while also importing assumptions.
concepts.insight: Map the comparison and identify where it stops working. A vivid metaphor does not establish all the facts its frame suggests.
concepts.example: Calling an archive “a conversation” emphasizes exchange, but records cannot literally answer every question.
concepts.misconception: A comparison is not proof merely because it is memorable.

project.title: A metaphor you can walk through
project.brief: Build and critique a spatial metaphor for a public issue.
project.composition: Write an argument organized by one metaphor and a counterargument exposing its limits.
project.visual: Create a walk-through drawing or tabletop model with labeled correspondences.
project.analysis: Explain which features transfer and which misleadingly travel with the metaphor.
project.argument: Revise the argument with a bounded comparison.
project.reflection: Which part of the metaphor became more persuasive than the evidence warranted?

practice.passage: Original fictional editorial: “A square is the town’s living room. Yet unlike a private living room, it must welcome people its regular users have not invited.”

read.stem: The second sentence primarily
options: qualifies the metaphor to emphasize public inclusion.
rejects all shared space.
proves the square is inside a house.
argues that strangers should be excluded.
rationales: It identifies a consequential difference from a private room.
The writer supports a more inclusive space.
The comparison is figurative.
It argues the opposite.

write.stem: Which extension best preserves the bounded metaphor?
options: Only the owner may enter.
The square needs a television in every corner.
All towns are exactly like houses.
Its seating should make gathering possible without treating newcomers as intruders.
rationales: That imports a private-property feature the writer rejects.
The literal extension is irrelevant.
This erases the stated limit.
The sentence develops hospitality while respecting public access.

frq.prompt: Develop a position on what makes a shared space meaningfully public, using Bellweather’s proposal as the case.
frq.focus: Use a clear conceptual frame without letting a metaphor substitute for evidence.

concepts.title: Citation & intellectual responsibility
concepts.definition: Attribution distinguishes your reasoning from borrowed ideas and lets readers trace support. Identify the source of quotations, paraphrases, and borrowed data; accuracy matters as much as the presence of a citation.
concepts.insight: In a supplied synthesis packet, consistent labels such as Source B are usable. For outside research, include enough publication information and a link for retrieval.
concepts.example: A data claim followed by “(Source B)” should accurately represent the table and its limits.
concepts.misconception: Changing the wording does not remove the need to credit an idea.

project.title: The provenance trail
project.brief: Make every important factual claim traceable.
project.composition: Write a researched recommendation and a source audit that distinguishes evidence, inference, and uncertainty.
project.visual: Create a trail from each claim to a source excerpt and its context.
project.analysis: Explain where a secondary account altered the original claim.
project.argument: Defend which claims should be retained, revised, or removed.
project.reflection: Which citation looked complete but failed to support the sentence attached to it?

practice.passage: Original fictional draft: “The pilot recorded 260 visits with temporary seating. This proves residents support permanent construction.” The supplied observation table reports visits but does not measure opinions.

read.stem: The draft’s main source-use problem is that it
options: fails to quote every word of the table.
draws an opinion conclusion from a measure of visits.
uses a number that cannot appear in prose.
contains too much attribution.
rationales: Accurate paraphrase is permissible.
The cited outcome is behavior counted, not stated approval.
Numbers can be used in arguments.
The issue is the unsupported inference.

write.stem: Which revision is most responsible?
options: The pilot recorded 260 visits with seating (Source B), suggesting use worth investigating, though it did not measure support for construction.
Residents unanimously support construction (Source B).
The pilot proves everything we need.
Someone somewhere counted some visits.
rationales: It attributes the count and preserves the limit.
The citation does not support unanimity.
The broad claim lacks support.
Vague attribution prevents verification.

frq.prompt: Develop a position on what Bellweather can responsibly conclude from the six sources before committing funds to construction.
frq.focus: Make the origin and limits of every borrowed claim clear.

concepts.title: Primary & secondary sources
concepts.definition: A source’s role depends on the research question. Primary material offers direct evidence of the object or event being studied; secondary material interprets or synthesizes other evidence. Neither role alone guarantees accuracy, relevance, or fairness.
concepts.insight: Identify what you are trying to learn before classifying a source. A newspaper editorial is primary evidence of its own argument but may offer secondhand claims about an event. Examine access, purpose, methods, and omissions in either case.
concepts.example: Meeting minutes can document a recorded vote. A later historian’s account can explain how that vote fits a larger pattern. The minutes may still omit discussion, and the historian’s interpretation still needs support.
concepts.misconception: “Primary” does not mean unbiased or automatically better. A source close to an event can be mistaken, selective, or strategically framed.

project.title: The archive with two lenses
project.brief: Investigate an event through records and later interpretations.
project.composition: Choose a school or community event with accessible records. Assemble at least two direct records and two interpretations, or create a clearly labeled fictional dossier. Write a 600-word account and a source-role note explaining what each item can establish.
project.visual: Build a layered timeline distinguishing when events occurred, when records were produced, and when interpretations appeared. Add an accessible source index.
project.analysis: Explain six choices of quotation, placement, or omission. Show how the same document could change source roles under a different research question.
project.argument: Defend one contested interpretation while addressing a gap in the direct record. Revise after a peer checks whether each claim rests on a source capable of supporting it.
project.reflection: Which source seemed strongest because of its proximity to an event, and what did that proximity fail to guarantee?

practice.passage: Original fictional research note: “For a study of why a school garden was removed, the committee’s minutes record a vote but omit the discussion. A student newspaper editorial written that week criticizes the decision as wasteful. A retrospective article five years later uses interviews to connect the removal to a larger building plan. The editorial is direct evidence of a public response; its claim about the committee’s private motives still requires corroboration.”

read.stem: The final sentence most clearly distinguishes between
options: an official record that proves motives and an editorial that contains no useful evidence.
what a document directly demonstrates and what its claims require a researcher to verify elsewhere.
a document’s official status and its usefulness for establishing any claim about the event.
a contemporary source that must be accurate and a later source that must be unreliable.
rationales: The minutes omit discussion, while the editorial remains evidence of a response.
The editorial documents its own response, but it cannot alone establish another group’s private motives.
The contrast is about what a source can establish, not a ranking by official status.
The note makes no blanket reliability judgment based on age.

write.stem: The researcher wants to support a claim that the building plan influenced the removal decision. Which additional evidence would best serve that purpose?
options: A dated planning memo discussed before the vote that identifies the garden site as necessary for construction.
A recent photograph showing that the garden is no longer present.
A list of positive reactions to the student newspaper editorial.
An account of the garden’s popularity several years before the vote.
rationales: The memo could directly connect planning considerations to the decision process.
The photograph confirms removal, not the reason for it.
Responses to the editorial do not establish the committee’s planning considerations.
Earlier popularity does not demonstrate the building plan’s influence.

frq.prompt: Write an essay that develops your position on the most important considerations a town should weigh when deciding how to redesign a public square.
frq.focus: Distinguish what firsthand perspectives, quantitative records, and interpretive proposals in the packet can each establish.

concepts.title: Paraphrase & summary
concepts.definition: A paraphrase restates a particular passage in new wording and syntax while preserving its meaning. A summary condenses a larger text’s central ideas. Both require attribution, and neither permits silently changing scope, certainty, or viewpoint.
concepts.insight: Record the source’s claim, limits, and relationship among ideas before restating it. Then check your version against the original. Use quotation marks for wording you retain, and keep your evaluation distinct from what the source says.
concepts.example: “Some respondents preferred a trial” cannot become “Residents demanded permanent adoption.” The shift changes population, force, and duration, even if every word is different.
concepts.misconception: Swapping synonyms is not an adequate paraphrase. A citation acknowledges a source but does not make misleading restatement or unattributed copied language acceptable.

project.title: The compression studio
project.brief: Translate one argument into three lengths without losing its limits.
project.composition: Use a supplied source or a short openly available article. Produce a 200-word paraphrase of one section, a 100-word summary of the whole, and a 40-word public caption. Attribute each and keep a record of what was omitted.
project.visual: Make an accordion display linking the three versions to the original claim, evidence, and qualifications. Use a text key so no relationship depends only on color.
project.analysis: Analyze six decisions about compression, syntax, attribution, or emphasis. Identify one omission that would materially change the source’s position.
project.argument: Argue which details are indispensable for the chosen audience. Answer a reader who wants a shorter version, then revise after checking all three versions against the source.
project.reflection: At what point did compression stop preserving the source and begin replacing it with your own position?

practice.passage: Original fictional source and student draft: Source: “In interviews with 24 residents who had attended the pilot, 15 supported repeating it next summer, provided the town added shaded seating. The interviews do not establish whether residents who stayed away would support it.” Student draft: “Most residents want the pilot to become a permanent event.” The student wants to use the source to discuss support for another trial.

read.stem: Which problem most seriously weakens the student’s use of the source?
options: The source contains numerical evidence that cannot be summarized in prose.
The draft fails to explain why every interviewee attended the pilot.
The draft broadens the population and turns conditional support for repetition into support for permanence.
The draft uses different words from those in the source.
rationales: Numerical findings can be summarized accurately with their scope and limits.
Attendance motives are not necessary to identify the stated support and its limits.
It changes attendees to all residents, omits the shade condition, and changes the duration.
Different wording is expected in a paraphrase; distortion of meaning is the problem.

write.stem: Which revision best uses the source accurately to support discussion of another trial?
options: The report suggests that shade was the only reason residents missed the pilot.
According to the interview report, 15 of the 24 attendees interviewed favored repeating the pilot next summer if shaded seating were added.
The report proves that most town residents favor annual adoption after minor improvements.
The interviews show that all attendees would return if the town added shade.
rationales: The source expressly does not establish the preferences of people who stayed away.
The revision preserves the sample, finding, condition, and limited duration while attributing the report.
The claim still generalizes beyond attendees and replaces a conditional repeat with annual adoption.
Fifteen of 24 is not all, and support for repeating the event is not a promise to attend.

frq.prompt: Write an essay that develops your position on how a town should balance different residents’ needs when redesigning a public square.
frq.focus: Paraphrase at least two sources without expanding their claims, and make clear where your reasoning begins.

concepts.title: Qualification & scope
concepts.definition: Qualification specifies the conditions, degree, or population for which a claim holds. It makes a position more accurate without requiring indecision.
concepts.insight: Identify the evidence boundary, then choose a meaningful limit. Words such as “sometimes” help only if the argument explains when and why.
concepts.example: A trial may be useful when the decision is reversible and its risks can be contained.
concepts.misconception: Qualifying a claim does not mean refusing to take a position.

project.title: The claim with adjustable edges
project.brief: Find the strongest defensible scope of a position.
project.composition: Write a bold policy claim, test three difficult cases, and develop a qualified revision.
project.visual: Create a map with movable boundaries marking where the claim applies.
project.analysis: Explain the evidence behind each boundary.
project.argument: Defend a firm recommendation within the justified conditions.
project.reflection: Which limit strengthened your position rather than weakening it?

practice.passage: Original fictional argument: “Shared tools can reduce costs for clubs with similar needs, provided that maintenance responsibilities are clear.”

read.stem: The qualifications restrict the claim by
options: claiming identical results everywhere.
changing the subject to unrelated tools.
identifying suitable users and an implementation condition.
denying any possible benefit.
rationales: The conditions reject that scope.
The subject remains shared equipment.
Similar needs and maintenance duties bound the benefit.
The benefit remains asserted conditionally.

write.stem: Which revision most responsibly strengthens the claim?
options: Maintenance never matters.
For clubs that use the same equipment intermittently, a maintained lending pool can reduce duplicate purchases.
All sharing always saves money.
Sharing may or may not be something.
rationales: This discards a relevant condition.
The revision specifies a mechanism and scope.
The absolute claim exceeds the conditions.
The vagueness removes a defensible position.

frq.prompt: Sharing resources is often presented as an efficient alternative to individual ownership. Develop an argument about the conditions under which shared ownership is beneficial.
frq.focus: Specify consequential conditions while maintaining a clear position.

concepts.title: Counterargument & alternative perspectives
concepts.definition: A counterargument challenges a claim, its support, its assumptions, or its consequences. Address the strongest relevant objection rather than a convenient caricature.
concepts.insight: Represent the objection so a reasonable opponent would recognize it. Explain how it changes your reasoning or why your position still holds.
