concepts.example: A critic of longer library hours may raise staffing burdens rather than oppose access itself.
concepts.misconception: Mentioning “some people disagree” does not develop a counterargument.

project.title: The objection that matters
project.brief: Let a serious opposing position improve your proposal.
project.composition: Write a policy brief and the strongest evidence-based objection to it.
project.visual: Design a debate board connecting objections to the exact claims they challenge.
project.analysis: Distinguish objections about goals, evidence, feasibility, and consequences.
project.argument: Revise the proposal or explain why its benefits still outweigh the objection.
project.reflection: Which criticism could you not answer without changing your plan?

practice.passage: Original fictional exchange: “Extend library hours,” a student proposes. A librarian replies, “Without additional staff funding, that would require unpaid work.”

read.stem: The reply challenges chiefly the proposal’s
options: belief that reading matters.
claim that libraries contain books.
assumption that all students dislike libraries.
implementation conditions.
rationales: No objection to reading is stated.
That fact is not disputed.
The proposal makes no such assumption.
The librarian raises how the change would be staffed.

write.stem: Which response best addresses the objection?
options: Ignore the staffing question until after approval.
Books are important.
Include paid staffing in the trial budget and adjust the hours to the available funds.
Librarians do not care about students.
rationales: This leaves the feasibility problem unresolved.
A shared value does not answer the cost objection.
It responds to the actual labor concern.
This misrepresents the objection.

frq.prompt: A worthwhile public service can impose costs on the people who provide it. Develop an argument about how communities should balance expanded access with fair working conditions.
frq.focus: Develop a serious objection and respond to its actual reasoning.

concepts.title: Concession & rebuttal
concepts.definition: A concession grants a valid part of an opposing argument. A rebuttal responds by challenging an inference, adding context, weighing competing values, or revising the proposal.
concepts.insight: Specify exactly what is granted and what does not follow. The response should do more than pivot back to the original assertion.
concepts.example: “The trial costs money, but its limited duration lets us evaluate whether the benefit warrants continuing it” grants cost without abandoning the test.
concepts.misconception: “Yes, but” is not a substitute for an explanation.

project.title: The negotiated design
project.brief: Build a proposal that visibly changes after an objection.
project.composition: Write an initial recommendation, a fair concession, and a revised recommendation with a reasoned response.
project.visual: Create a layered blueprint showing what was retained and what changed.
project.analysis: Explain why the concession does not require surrendering the whole position.
project.argument: Defend the revised tradeoff to both sides.
project.reflection: What would count as evidence that your rebuttal is insufficient?

practice.passage: Original fictional argument: “The trial will not reproduce the shade of mature trees. Still, it can reveal whether the new paths interfere with deliveries. We should use it for that narrower purpose.”

read.stem: The writer responds to the limitation by
options: narrowing the trial’s purpose to what it can test.
denying the limitation exists.
claiming the trial tests everything.
changing to an unrelated policy.
rationales: The concession leads to a bounded use rather than abandonment.
The opening explicitly accepts it.
The purpose is narrowed.
The trial remains the subject.

write.stem: Which sentence best continues the rebuttal?
options: Therefore no other evidence is needed.
Critics should remain silent.
The trial is perfect.
A separate assessment would be needed to estimate the benefits of long-term shade.
rationales: This contradicts the acknowledged limitation.
This does not address the reasoning.
The absolute claim erases the concession.
The response accounts for the untested dimension.

frq.prompt: An imperfect experiment can still produce useful knowledge. Develop an argument about when limited trials are worth conducting.
frq.focus: Concede a real limitation and explain what remains justified.

concepts.title: Clauses & sentence boundaries
concepts.definition: Independent clauses can stand as sentences; dependent clauses cannot. Joining or separating clauses changes both grammatical clarity and the relationship readers perceive.
concepts.insight: Choose coordination for comparable weight and subordination when one idea should frame or qualify another. Repair errors in service of meaning.
concepts.example: “Although the trial is limited, it can test circulation” makes the limitation a frame for the main claim.
concepts.misconception: A comma alone does not usually join two independent clauses in standard edited prose.

project.title: The clause architecture studio
project.brief: Make grammatical relationships visible as spatial relationships.
project.composition: Write a policy argument, then revise ten sentences using deliberate coordination or subordination.
project.visual: Build clause floor plans with main rooms and dependent spaces.
project.analysis: Explain how each revision changes emphasis, concession, or causality.
project.argument: Defend the clearest version of a contested sentence.
project.reflection: Which grammatical revision changed your argument rather than just correcting it?

practice.passage: Original fictional sentence: “Although the archive is incomplete, it offers a foundation for further research.”

read.stem: Placing the limitation in a dependent clause
options: denies the archive has limits.
acknowledges it while giving the main emphasis to continued usefulness.
makes incompleteness the sole conclusion.
creates two unrelated complete sentences.
rationales: The first clause states a limit.
The main clause carries the positive claim.
The main clause adds a substantive benefit.
The clauses are grammatically connected.

write.stem: Which revision best combines these ideas as a concession: “The plan costs more. It improves access”?
options: Although the plan costs more, it improves access.
The plan costs more, it improves access.
Because the plan costs more, it improves access.
Although the plan costs more.
rationales: The subordinate clause concedes cost while emphasizing access.
The comma splice obscures the intended connection.
Cost alone is not established as the cause of access.
The dependent clause is left without a main clause.

frq.prompt: A more inclusive design may require greater initial expense. Develop an argument about the extent to which institutions should prioritize accessibility when allocating limited resources.
frq.focus: Use clause relationships to express your actual qualifications.

concepts.title: Punctuation & clarity
concepts.definition: Punctuation marks relationships and controls how a sentence unfolds. Colons introduce explanations or examples after a complete clause; semicolons can join closely related independent clauses; dashes can set off an interruption or emphasis.
concepts.insight: Read the relationship first, then choose the mark. Punctuation cannot repair a missing logical connection by itself.
concepts.example: “The issue is access: some residents cannot arrive before six” introduces an explanation.
concepts.misconception: Sophistication does not require frequent semicolons or dashes.

project.title: The punctuation scorecard
project.brief: Show how marks change the reading of a public statement.
project.composition: Compose a statement and three punctuated versions of a crucial paragraph.
project.visual: Create a performance score with pauses and relationships marked visually.
project.analysis: Explain which marks clarify, subordinate, or interrupt ideas.
project.argument: Defend a version for both silent reading and oral delivery.
project.reflection: Where did a dramatic pause create an unintended ambiguity?

practice.passage: Original fictional sentence: “The archive needs one thing above all: permission from the people whose stories it preserves.”

read.stem: The colon primarily
options: signals that the preceding clause is a question.
marks a quotation from an unnamed source.
introduces a specification of the preceding phrase.
separates unrelated claims.
rationales: The sentence is declarative.
No quotation is indicated.
What follows identifies the “one thing.”
The second part directly explains the first.

write.stem: Which version most clearly joins two related independent clauses?
options: The records: are incomplete further interviews may fill the gaps.
The records are incomplete; further interviews may fill the gaps.
The records are incomplete, further interviews may fill the gaps.
The records are; incomplete further interviews may fill the gaps.
rationales: The colon interrupts the predicate and leaves the clauses unjoined.
Both clauses are complete and closely connected.
A comma alone creates a splice in edited prose.
The semicolon interrupts the first clause.

frq.prompt: Collecting a person’s story can preserve history while raising questions about control. Develop an argument about the responsibilities of people who collect and share others’ experiences.
frq.focus: Use punctuation to make the relationships among your claims unambiguous.

concepts.title: Parallelism & antithesis
concepts.definition: Parallel structure gives comparable ideas a similar grammatical form. Antithesis places contrasting ideas in a balanced relationship. Both can sharpen distinctions or imply equivalence that readers should examine.
concepts.insight: Identify what the form equates or contrasts. Ask whether the relationship is justified, not merely pleasing to hear.
concepts.example: “Count the cost. Count the users. Count the people excluded” gives three considerations comparable emphasis.
concepts.misconception: Balanced syntax does not guarantee balanced reasoning.

project.title: The balanced-line broadside
project.brief: Use and critique the persuasive force of balance.
project.composition: Write two public statements, one using justified parallelism and one exposing a misleading equivalence.
project.visual: Design a typographic broadside that visually balances the paired claims.
project.analysis: Analyze how form influences perceived weight and contrast.
project.argument: Defend the relationship your final parallel structure establishes.
project.reflection: Which attractive balance concealed an important difference?

practice.passage: Original fictional statement: “We need the announcement and the experience, the map and the journey, the official record and the ordinary day.”

read.stem: The repeated paired structure primarily
options: proves the paired items are identical.
dismisses all official records.
removes any relation among the examples.
gives complementary kinds of knowledge comparable importance.
rationales: Complementarity is not identity.
The statement says both are needed.
The repeated form establishes a common relation.
Each pair joins institutional representation with lived experience.

write.stem: Which revision maintains clear parallel form?
options: The project should documentation and preserve and gaps.
The project decisions, testimony, identify.
The project should document decisions, preserve testimony, and identify gaps.
The project should document decisions, testimony preservation, and gaps are identified.
rationales: The sequence lacks coherent parallel verbs and objects.
The fragment does not express the intended actions.
The three verb phrases share a grammatical pattern.
The forms do not align.

frq.prompt: Official records and personal accounts often reveal different aspects of an event. Develop an argument about the value of preserving both kinds of knowledge.
frq.focus: Use balanced language only where the underlying relationship warrants it.

concepts.title: Emphasis & sentence placement
concepts.definition: Placement controls what readers encounter first, what they must hold in mind, and what receives final emphasis. Periodic sentences delay a main clause; cumulative sentences add detail after it.
concepts.insight: Compare alternative placements and explain the interpretive difference. Emphasis should highlight an argument’s real priorities.
concepts.example: A sentence can first concede budget constraints and end with the people those constraints affect.
concepts.misconception: The last word does not mechanically determine every reader’s interpretation.

project.title: The last-word installation
project.brief: Make sentence placement serve a hierarchy of ideas.
project.composition: Write an argument and revise its key sentences to test different positions for the central claim.
project.visual: Arrange text on hanging panels so readers encounter clauses in a deliberate order.
project.analysis: Explain what is delayed, foregrounded, or left resonating.
project.argument: Defend the arrangement that makes your priority clearest without hiding a limitation.
project.reflection: Which delayed detail proved too important to leave until the end?

practice.passage: Original fictional sentence: “After the estimates are checked, after staff are consulted, and after access is reviewed, the council should begin a trial.”

read.stem: Delaying the main clause emphasizes
options: the conditions that must precede the recommendation.
that consultation should occur only after construction.
that the council should never act.
that all conditions are irrelevant.
rationales: Readers pass through safeguards before reaching the action.
The conditions precede the trial.
The sentence ends with a recommendation.
Their prominent placement suggests importance.

write.stem: Which revision gives the action immediate emphasis while retaining the conditions?
options: Begin immediately and ignore all reviews.
Costs and staffing and access.
After review.
Begin a trial once costs, staffing, and access have been reviewed.
rationales: This changes the meaning.
The fragment omits the action.
The fragment omits both the action and the review’s scope.
The imperative appears first; conditions remain explicit.

frq.prompt: Careful preparation can improve action but can also delay it. Develop an argument about how groups should decide when they have enough information to begin.
frq.focus: Make your hierarchy of conditions and actions visible in sentence structure.

concepts.title: Antithesis
concepts.definition: Antithesis places contrasting ideas in a balanced relationship, often using parallel syntax. It can clarify a distinction, sharpen a choice, or expose a tension; its persuasiveness still depends on whether the contrast is fair.
concepts.insight: Name the ideas being contrasted and inspect the grammar that places them in relation. Ask what the balance highlights, what it leaves outside the comparison, and whether the argument treats a spectrum as only two alternatives.
concepts.example: “We need a room for listening, not a stage for agreement” contrasts two purposes for a public meeting. The sentence invites scrutiny of whether listening and agreement must actually conflict.
concepts.misconception: Balanced opposites are not evidence that only two choices exist. Antithesis can be useful without pretending that the contrast exhausts the issue.

project.title: The balanced poster debate
project.brief: Create a memorable contrast and then test its fairness.
project.composition: Write two 450-word position pieces about how a school should recognize achievement. Give each a central antithetical sentence. Produce a revised version that keeps the contrast while acknowledging a meaningful overlap.
project.visual: Design a two-panel poster plus a movable third panel for cases that resist the binary. Include equivalent text for all panels.
project.analysis: Analyze six choices of parallel structure, word order, placement, or scale. Explain how visual balance makes the opposition appear more complete than it may be.
project.argument: Defend the distinction your poster makes while addressing a case that fits both sides. Revise the slogan and one paragraph so the exception affects the proposal.
project.reflection: What did the third panel reveal that the original balanced design encouraged readers to overlook?

practice.passage: Original fictional editorial: “A public consultation should be a place to test a proposal, not a ceremony to celebrate it. That does not mean praise is useless. It means the meeting must make room for evidence that might change the plan. If the only permitted response is applause, the decision has already happened somewhere else.”

read.stem: The balanced contrast in the first sentence primarily
options: claims that participants who praise a proposal cannot offer useful evidence.
contrasts the architectural designs of two kinds of meeting rooms.
suggests that public consultation should end whenever agreement is possible.
distinguishes deliberation that can change a plan from participation that merely endorses it.
rationales: The next sentence explicitly preserves a role for praise.
“Place” and “ceremony” describe purposes, not building plans.
The concern is a process that excludes criticism, not agreement itself.
Testing permits revision; celebrating alone presents approval as the meeting’s purpose.

write.stem: The writer wants to preserve a balanced contrast without implying that support and scrutiny cannot coexist. Which sentence best replaces the first sentence?
options: A consultation should be public, useful, scheduled, and well attended.
A consultation can be a celebration because any approval demonstrates careful reasoning.
A consultation should welcome support while testing its grounds, not demand support while forbidding its examination.
A consultation must choose between agreement and honest inquiry.
rationales: The list removes the relevant contrast without clarifying the purpose.
This equates approval with scrutiny and contradicts the passage’s concern.
The parallel phrasing contrasts open and closed processes while allowing support within scrutiny.
This intensifies the false opposition the writer wants to avoid.

frq.focus: Examine how the speaker uses contrasts between administrative completion and visitor access without dismissing the staff’s work.

concepts.title: Modality & hedging
concepts.definition: Modality expresses a writer’s stance toward possibility, certainty, obligation, or permission through words such as “may,” “must,” and “should.” Hedging limits commitment when evidence or conditions do not justify an unrestricted claim.
concepts.insight: Distinguish uncertainty about whether something is true from a judgment about what ought to happen. “May reduce delays” and “should reduce delays” can do different work. Choose the degree of certainty that your evidence permits.
concepts.example: “A shared calendar may reduce clashes when organizers enter events promptly” makes both the prediction and its condition visible.
concepts.misconception: Hedging is not adding “perhaps” to every sentence. Unsupported certainty and vague evasiveness both make an argument harder to evaluate.

project.title: The certainty dial
project.brief: Show how a change in certainty changes a public recommendation.
project.composition: Create a small fictional pilot report with explicitly simulated results and clear limits. Write a 450-word cautious recommendation and a 450-word assertive recommendation grounded in the same report. Keep a log of every certainty or obligation marker.
project.visual: Build a dial or graduated strip connecting claim strength to supporting evidence and conditions. Provide the full labels in a text table.
project.analysis: Analyze six changes in modality. Identify whether each expresses likelihood, duty, permission, or a limit, and explain the possible audience effect.
project.argument: Defend the strongest wording your report supports. Address a reader who wants a definitive answer, then revise both overstatement and unnecessary hesitation.
project.reflection: Which hedge protected accuracy, and which merely concealed a claim you had not decided how to defend?

practice.passage: Original fictional pilot report: “During two trial weeks, the shared calendar coincided with fewer room-booking conflicts. Organizers entered events voluntarily, and two large clubs did not participate. The calendar may help reduce conflicts when most organizers keep it current. The school should expand participation for another month before deciding whether to require it.”

read.stem: The phrase “may help” chiefly qualifies the report’s claim by
options: presenting a possible contribution without asserting that the calendar alone caused the improvement.
denying that any improvement occurred during the trial.
making calendar participation a mandatory obligation for every club.
establishing that the calendar will work equally well in every setting.
rationales: The brief voluntary trial supports a cautious inference, especially with incomplete participation.
The report states that fewer conflicts occurred.
The phrase concerns possible effect; a requirement remains under consideration.
The phrase and following condition limit, rather than universalize, the prediction.

write.stem: Which revision best preserves an evidence-based limit while making the report’s recommendation more precise?
options: The school must require the calendar immediately because it has eliminated booking conflicts.
The school could continue gathering information without identifying which groups or outcomes the next stage should examine.
The school should end the trial because incomplete participation proves the calendar ineffective.
The school should invite the two absent clubs into a month-long extension and compare conflicts before considering a requirement.
rationales: The trial showed fewer conflicts, not elimination or a proven cause.
This expresses caution but leaves the study design and decision criteria less precise.
Incomplete participation limits the evidence but does not prove ineffectiveness.
The revision identifies a missing group, a next step, and a decision condition.

frq.prompt: Public audiences often reward confident recommendations even when the available evidence is incomplete. Write an essay that argues your position on the responsibilities of a writer communicating uncertainty while calling for action.
frq.focus: Distinguish uncertainty about effects from the strength of a recommendation.

concepts.title: Audience adaptation & rhetorical transfer
concepts.definition: Adaptation changes the choices a text makes when its audience or situation changes. Preserve factual integrity while reconsidering context, register, support, medium, and the action readers can take.
concepts.insight: Ask what the new audience knows, values, doubts, and controls. A shorter text may require a different structure, not just fewer words.
concepts.example: A proposal to administrators may foreground implementation; a message to students may explain participation.
concepts.misconception: Audience adaptation does not authorize presenting incompatible facts to different groups.

project.title: The three-channel public notice
project.brief: Carry one position across audiences and media.
project.composition: Compose a formal proposal, a student-facing article, and a spoken announcement about notification policy.
project.visual: Create a visual identity that changes hierarchy for each format.
project.analysis: Analyze what you explained, omitted, or reorganized and why.
project.argument: Defend the version that best serves a skeptical audience.
project.reflection: Which change preserved your purpose while substantially altering the form?

practice.passage: Original fictional proposal to administrators: “Allow students to choose reminder intervals. A pilot can compare missed assignments and reported interruptions before a schoolwide decision.”

read.stem: The proposal addresses administrators chiefly by
options: discussing only decorative app features.
offering a measurable way to evaluate a policy change.
assuming they share every student’s preferences.
asking them to ignore outcomes.
rationales: The focus is policy and evaluation.
The pilot links the request to decision criteria.
The proposal calls for evidence rather than assuming agreement.
Outcomes are explicit.

write.stem: For a student audience, which addition best adapts the message?
options: During the pilot, record which reminders help and which interrupt your work.
Students should approve the district budget directly.
The pilot is guaranteed to solve every problem.
Administrative regulations are always meaningless.
rationales: It gives students a relevant participatory action.
The action may exceed their authority.
The guarantee is unsupported.
The dismissal does not clarify the student role.

frq.focus: Explain how Ellis addresses students while implicitly challenging administrators’ criteria.

concepts.title: Style & voice
concepts.definition: Style is the pattern of choices across a text; voice is the impression of a speaking presence those choices create. Both arise from more than a single device or adjective.
concepts.insight: Track recurring diction, rhythms, stance, and relationships with readers. Explain how the pattern serves the argument.
concepts.example: A mock official announcement can sound ceremonious while exposing the absurdity of its policy.
concepts.misconception: An authentic voice need not resemble casual speech.

project.title: The voice studio
project.brief: Construct distinct voices without caricaturing their beliefs.
project.composition: Write three positions on attention technology for three defined audiences, choosing a coherent style for each.
project.visual: Design a three-panel score of recurring words, rhythms, and visual motifs.
project.analysis: Explain how each voice gains credibility and where it risks alienating readers.
project.argument: Defend the stylistic choice best suited to a particular situation.
project.reflection: Which voice required the deepest revision of your assumptions?

practice.passage: Original fictional satire: “The committee is pleased to announce that its new focus reminder will interrupt your work every seven minutes.”

read.stem: The sentence’s voice depends on the contrast between
options: technical accuracy and a missing date.
informal slang and intimate confession.
official approval language and a self-defeating action.
two identical views of productivity.
rationales: The irony does not depend on a date.
The sentence uses formal institutional language.
The ceremonial announcement clashes with interruption in the name of focus.
The conflict is between stated goal and method.

write.stem: Which sentence best sustains that voice?
options: Students should evaluate whether the reminders are useful before adopting them.
To ensure you are concentrating, we will require frequent confirmation clicks.
Hey, this app is kinda annoying.
The reminder system is a neutral technical object.
rationales: The direct, sensible recommendation abandons the mock institutional persona and its ironic contradiction.
The formal assurance continues the self-defeating logic.
The casual register changes the constructed voice.
This removes the satirical contradiction.

frq.focus: Explain how an institutional persona lets the writer expose a policy’s contradictions.

concepts.title: Irony & satire
concepts.definition: Irony creates a gap between stated and implied meaning or between expectations and outcomes. Satire uses humor, exaggeration, or ironic distance to criticize a target.
concepts.insight: Identify the target and the standard implied by the criticism. Explain how readers are invited to detect the gap; do not assume every funny line is satire.
concepts.example: A “focus” tool that demands constant clicks exposes a conflict between measurable activity and concentration.
concepts.misconception: The literal speaker’s claim may not be the writer’s endorsed position.

project.title: The department of helpful obstacles
project.brief: Invent a satirical institution whose procedures undermine its stated mission.
project.composition: Write a mock policy announcement and a serious proposal addressing the same problem.
project.visual: Design an institutional seal and flowchart that expose the contradiction.
project.analysis: Analyze the gap between literal claims and implied criticism.
project.argument: Defend the serious remedy and explain what satire could not establish alone.
project.reflection: Where could a reader mistake the satire for endorsement?

practice.passage: Original fictional satire: “Students who find the notifications distracting may silence them by completing a mandatory ten-minute focus survey every hour.”

read.stem: The satire targets
options: the idea that no student ever needs reminders.
the length of all school days.
students’ inability to read surveys.
a remedy that reproduces the problem it claims to solve.
rationales: The sentence does not establish that universal criticism.
The target is the notification remedy.
Reading ability is not the stated contradiction.
The mandatory survey creates another interruption.

write.stem: Which addition sharpens the same satirical target?
options: Surveys have questions.
All technology is evil.
The survey will ask why you have not finished your work.
Students sometimes use paper notebooks.
rationales: The observation is literal and uncritical.
The sweeping assertion loses the specific target.
It exposes the system blaming users for its own interruptions.
The fact does not extend the contradiction.

frq.focus: Identify the satirical target precisely and analyze the shift into direct qualification.

concepts.title: Rhetorical questions & reader positioning
concepts.definition: A rhetorical question invites reflection, implies an answer, challenges an assumption, or directs readers toward a judgment. It can open inquiry or constrain the range of acceptable responses.
concepts.insight: Ask what answer the surrounding text makes likely and why that matters to the audience. Compare with a direct assertion.
concepts.example: “What have we measured if we have counted every click but no understanding?” challenges a metric’s relevance.
concepts.misconception: A question mark does not guarantee openness to disagreement.

project.title: The question corridor
project.brief: Guide readers through a problem while testing the fairness of your questions.
project.composition: Write an interrogative editorial and a direct-assertion version of the same argument.
project.visual: Design a corridor of question panels with possible response paths.
project.analysis: Identify loaded premises and places where real alternatives are excluded.
project.argument: Defend a revised sequence that invites judgment without misrepresenting options.
project.reflection: Which question gave the illusion of choice?

practice.passage: Original fictional editorial: “If a student clicks every reminder but learns nothing, what exactly has the system measured?”

read.stem: The question primarily challenges
options: the assumption that measured compliance demonstrates learning.
the existence of students.
the possibility of measuring anything.
the need to read instructions.
rationales: The hypothetical separates clicking from understanding.
The question assumes a student exists.
It targets one measure’s meaning.
Instruction-reading is not the issue.

write.stem: Which follow-up best develops the implied criticism?
options: All measurements must be abandoned.
Students should click faster.
The system should publish more detailed counts of reminder clicks.
Evaluation should include evidence of understanding, not just interaction counts.
rationales: This exceeds the targeted criticism.
This intensifies the inadequate measure.
More precise compliance counts would not establish the understanding the question distinguishes from clicking.
It supplies a relevant alternative criterion.

frq.focus: Explain how implicit questions about measurement guide readers toward the column’s final proposal.

concepts.title: Repetition & rhetorical pattern
concepts.definition: Repetition can connect ideas, build momentum, or make a pattern difficult to ignore. Anaphora repeats openings; other recurring words or images can develop meaning across a whole text.
concepts.insight: Explain what changes around the repeated element. Repetition is most interesting when each recurrence adds pressure, scope, or contrast.
concepts.example: Repeated “count” can broaden a budget debate from expenses to excluded people.
concepts.misconception: Repeating a claim does not add independent evidence.

project.title: The refrain with a changing meaning
project.brief: Build an argument around a phrase whose significance develops.
project.composition: Write a spoken argument with a recurring line and a prose version without it.
project.visual: Create a sequence of panels in which a repeated image changes context.
project.analysis: Explain what each recurrence adds and where repetition becomes empty.
project.argument: Defend the form that best supports the claim.
project.reflection: Which repetition earned emphasis, and which merely demanded agreement?

practice.passage: Original fictional statement: “Count the reminders. Count the clicks. Count the minutes in which no student could finish a thought.”

read.stem: The repeated imperative develops the argument by
options: praising reminders without qualification.
turning a familiar counting practice toward its overlooked cost.
offering three identical statistics.
showing that all counting is impossible.
rationales: The final clause exposes a cost.
The final object changes what deserves measurement.
No statistics are given, and the objects differ.
The speaker uses counting as a critical tool.

write.stem: Which concluding repetition best extends the pattern?
options: Count what the system interrupts as well as what it records.
Count, count, count, count.
All counts are equally meaningful.
Count every successful login as another instance of learning.
rationales: It states the broader evaluative principle.
Bare repetition adds no developed meaning.
This contradicts the distinction being made.
The sentence reproduces the questionable equivalence between interaction and understanding.

frq.focus: Analyze repeated institutional assurances and the changing judgments they invite.

concepts.title: Sentence variety & rhythm
concepts.definition: Variety in sentence length and structure can manage pace and emphasis. The goal is a meaningful relationship between rhythm and thought, not variation for its own sake.
concepts.insight: Read the paragraph aloud and identify where the reasoning needs acceleration, pause, contrast, or accumulation.
concepts.example: A list of bureaucratic procedures followed by “Nothing was learned” can expose the gap between activity and outcome.
concepts.misconception: Every paragraph does not need one sentence of each grammatical type.

project.title: The argument in tempo
project.brief: Translate a reasoning sequence into a deliberate rhythm.
project.composition: Write a speech and a silent-reading essay on the same issue with different sentence patterns.
project.visual: Create a visual tempo score linking sentence lengths to argumentative moves.
project.analysis: Analyze where pacing changes comprehension or emphasis.
project.argument: Defend the version best suited to its medium.
project.reflection: Which rhythmic flourish made a relationship harder to follow?

practice.passage: Original fictional satire: “The system logged each click, counted every pause, and issued a report with twelve charts. No one read it.”

read.stem: The short final sentence primarily
options: confirms the report’s universal influence.
makes the report’s existence uncertain.
undercuts the preceding accumulation of administrative activity.
adds another detailed measurement.
rationales: The sentence says it was unread.
The report is explicitly described.
The abrupt ending exposes a lack of meaningful use.
It states an outcome without elaboration.

write.stem: Which ending best preserves the same rhythmic effect?
options: Because the report.
Nothing changed.
The report, which was generated through several processes, contained numerous sections.
The unread report was nevertheless counted as another successful output.
rationales: The fragment does not communicate the intended outcome.
A brief sentence sharply contrasts activity with outcome.
This continues elaboration instead of undercutting it.
The idea extends the satire, but its explanatory continuation does not preserve the abrupt rhythmic contrast requested.

frq.focus: Explain how accumulation and abrupt statements expose the gap between activity and understanding.

concepts.title: Revision for purpose & coherence
concepts.definition: Revision reconsiders an argument’s purpose, support, organization, and style. Editing corrects local expression; both matter, but polishing cannot fix an unsupported central claim.
concepts.insight: Prioritize the change with the greatest effect on meaning. Use a reverse outline, evidence audit, and audience test before sentence-level polishing.
concepts.example: Replacing “everyone benefits” with a supported, conditional claim changes the reasoning, not just the wording.
concepts.misconception: A longer draft is not necessarily a more developed draft.

project.title: The revision palimpsest
project.brief: Make substantive changes visible instead of hiding the process.
project.composition: Draft an argument, collect reader feedback, and produce a revision with a decision log.
project.visual: Create a layered page showing deleted assumptions and rebuilt connections.
project.analysis: Explain three changes in reasoning and two changes in expression.
project.argument: Defend one suggestion you rejected using the purpose and evidence.
project.reflection: Which revision changed what you believed, and which only changed how you said it?

practice.passage: Original fictional draft: “All students need identical reminders because one student said notifications helped. Therefore the school should require them.”

read.stem: The draft’s most serious weakness is
options: the absence of a decorative opening.
the use of ordinary vocabulary.
the number of sentences alone.
a universal recommendation based on a single person’s experience.
rationales: Decoration would not repair the inference.
Plain wording is not the problem.
Length does not determine evidentiary adequacy.
The evidence does not establish identical needs.

write.stem: Which revision should come first?
options: Add three exclamation marks.
Repeat the anecdote at the end.
Investigate varied needs and revise the universal claim accordingly.
Replace ordinary words with longer synonyms.
rationales: Emphasis does not add support.
Repetition leaves the generalization unsupported.
This addresses the central evidence-to-claim mismatch.
Vocabulary changes do not repair the reasoning.

frq.focus: Explain how the direct qualification in paragraph 4 prevents the satire from becoming an indiscriminate attack.

concepts.title: Allusion & shared knowledge
concepts.definition: An allusion evokes another text, event, figure, or cultural story without fully retelling it. It invites readers to transfer associations to the present argument, depending on what they recognize and how they interpret that reference.
concepts.insight: Explain the relevant connection rather than merely naming the source. Consider readers who recognize it differently or not at all. An allusion can compress a comparison, establish affiliation, or challenge an inherited story.
concepts.example: Calling a constantly restarted cleanup “a task for Sisyphus” evokes repeated labor without lasting progress. The comparison needs enough context to work for readers unfamiliar with the myth.
concepts.misconception: An allusion is not automatically authoritative evidence. Familiarity can make a comparison memorable without proving that the situations are alike.

project.title: The shared-reference cabinet
project.brief: Test what a cultural reference includes, compresses, and excludes.
project.composition: Write a 500-word argument about a recurring local problem using one public-domain allusion. Create a second version for readers unfamiliar with it. Add a brief, accurately sourced explanation of the original reference.
project.visual: Design a pair of visual cabinets: one organizes the allusion’s associations, the other shows the literal situation. Connect only the parallels you can defend; include a text key.
project.analysis: Analyze six choices in explanation, imagery, or placement. Identify where the reference might invite an inference the real situation does not support.
project.argument: Defend whether the allusion should remain for the named audience. Address the strongest objection about exclusion or distortion, then revise after a reader attempts to explain the connection.
project.reflection: What did a reader unfamiliar with the reference notice that a knowledgeable reader might accept too quickly?

practice.passage: Original fictional editorial: “Each Friday we clear litter from the stream; each Monday more arrives from the uncovered bins upstream. Our cleanup has begun to resemble Sisyphus pushing his stone uphill only to watch it roll back down. The comparison has a limit: our task need not last forever. Replacing the bin lids would not make cleanup unnecessary, but it could stop us from beginning at the same point every week.”

read.stem: The allusion to Sisyphus primarily helps the writer
options: demonstrate through historical evidence that bin lids reduce pollution.
characterize the repetitive frustration of the cleanup before distinguishing the possibility of changing its cause.
argue that any attempt to clean the stream is inherently pointless.
establish that the volunteers are responsible for creating the litter.
rationales: A mythic allusion is not empirical evidence about bin lids.
The myth supplies a pattern of repeated labor; the next sentence limits the comparison.
The proposal preserves cleanup while addressing a recurring source of litter.
The passage identifies uncovered upstream bins, not volunteer misconduct.

write.stem: The writer wants to retain the allusion while making it accessible to readers unfamiliar with the myth. Which revision best achieves that goal?
options: Like Sisyphus, condemned in the Greek myth to push uphill a stone that repeatedly rolls back down, we keep repeating work undone at its source.
Our cleanup is Sisyphean in the most classical sense of that expression.
Sisyphus appears in Greek mythology alongside many other memorable figures.
Because ancient stories are always true, Sisyphus proves that our cleanup will fail.
rationales: The sentence supplies the relevant story and explicitly connects it to the present problem.
The specialized adjective assumes the very knowledge the writer wants to supply.
The background does not explain the relevant repeated task.
The revision misuses the allusion as proof and removes the original limitation.

frq.prompt: Writers often rely on shared cultural references to make an argument vivid or concise. Write an essay that argues your position on the value and limitations of this practice when addressing a diverse public audience.
frq.focus: Consider what a reference explains, what it assumes, and what it may distort.

concepts.title: Understatement & hyperbole
concepts.definition: Understatement deliberately represents something as less intense or significant than context suggests. Hyperbole deliberately exaggerates beyond literal accuracy. Both can shape attitude, expose a mismatch, or invite a reader to judge the gap between expression and situation.
concepts.insight: Establish the literal situation before interpreting the distortion. Explain how a particular audience can recognize the gap and why it matters. Exaggeration that readers reasonably take as factual may mislead rather than create a shared rhetorical effect.
concepts.example: After a committee sends twelve reminders in an hour, calling the inbox “a little busy” understates the burden; saying it “could bury the building” exaggerates it.
concepts.misconception: Understatement is not simply politeness, and every false claim is not hyperbole. Context must support the intended nonliteral reading.

project.title: The scale of the complaint
project.brief: Represent the same inconvenience literally and nonliterally.
project.composition: Write a 450-word literal policy complaint and a 450-word satirical column about a low-stakes routine. Use understatement and hyperbole in the column while keeping the actual problem recoverable. Label invented circumstances.
project.visual: Make a triptych with literal, minimized, and exaggerated representations. Include a text description and identify which visual changes alter scale rather than evidence.
project.analysis: Analyze six textual and visual distortions. Explain the cues that let readers reconstruct the real complaint and identify one distortion likely to mislead.
project.argument: Defend the version most useful for changing the policy. Address the risk that humor trivializes the problem, then revise a passage after checking what a reader believes actually happened.
project.reflection: When did a memorable exaggeration draw attention away from the action you wanted readers to consider?

practice.passage: Original fictional satirical column: “The new study app sent twelve reminders during my first hour of homework. This was a modest contribution to the atmosphere. By the fourth reminder I had learned the most important lesson: no thought should be left uninterrupted long enough to become an idea. Perhaps the next update can finish my sentences before I begin them.”

read.stem: The phrase “a modest contribution to the atmosphere” primarily
options: concedes that the reminders were too infrequent to affect the writer.
praises the app for helping the writer complete a difficult idea.
understates the interruption established by the preceding detail, creating an ironic contrast.
reports a measured improvement in the room’s physical conditions.
rationales: The following sentences criticize repeated interruption.
The passage instead implies that interruptions obstruct sustained thought.
Twelve reminders in an hour make the restrained description conspicuously inadequate.
“Atmosphere” refers to the study experience; no environmental measurement is given.

write.stem: The writer wants to end with hyperbole that sharpens the complaint about excessive reminders. Which sentence best achieves this goal?
options: Some users may prefer a different background color for the app.
At this rate, the app will need to send reminders reminding its reminders to leave room for homework.
The app sends reminders while students complete their homework.
A study has proved that every user loses half a letter grade each week.
rationales: The observation shifts to an unrelated preference.
The impossible recursion exaggerates notification overload while keeping the complaint recognizable.
The literal description removes the proposed exaggeration.
This invents an empirical finding that readers could mistake for factual evidence.

frq.focus: Explain how recognizable exaggerations and restrained descriptions help the column question its fictional policy.

concepts.title: Independent argument
concepts.definition: An independent argument answers a debatable question with a defensible position, specific support, and connected reasoning. Evidence may come from reading, history, observation, or experience, but should remain accurate and relevant.
concepts.insight: Define the task before choosing examples. Explain what each case establishes and consider a condition under which your position needs adjustment.
concepts.example: An argument about persistence should distinguish productive effort from continuing a demonstrably harmful course.
concepts.misconception: A collection of famous names does not substitute for developed evidence.

project.title: The public argument studio
project.brief: Develop a position that can survive a serious public response.
project.composition: Write a long-form argument, an opposing response, and a revised public version.
project.visual: Create an illustrated broadside that preserves the argument’s key qualification.
project.analysis: Analyze how medium and audience change the presentation of evidence.
project.argument: Defend the final position in a short question-and-answer transcript.
project.reflection: Which challenge changed your criteria for a successful argument?

practice.passage: Original fictional argument: “Persistence matters when feedback can improve the work. When repeated attempts reproduce the same harm, changing course may be the more responsible form of commitment.”

read.stem: The writer’s position is that persistence
options: should be evaluated in relation to learning and consequences.
is always harmful.
requires ignoring feedback.
has no relation to responsibility.
rationales: The writer distinguishes useful effort from repeated harm.
The opening affirms its value under conditions.
Feedback is central to productive persistence.
The conclusion explicitly invokes responsibility.

write.stem: Which evidence would most directly develop the distinction?
options: A list of unrelated successful people.
A claim that effort always wins.
A dictionary entry alone.
A detailed case in which feedback led a group to revise an unsuccessful approach.
rationales: Names without developed cases do not establish the mechanism.
The absolute assertion ignores the qualification.
A definition alone cannot establish the consequences.
The case illustrates learning-guided commitment.

frq.prompt: Persistence is often praised as a key to achievement. Develop an argument about the extent to which changing course can be a form of responsible commitment.
frq.focus: Develop specific evidence and a consequential distinction.

concepts.title: Complexity & sophistication
concepts.definition: Complexity emerges when an argument examines a consequential tension, limitation, or relationship instead of flattening the issue. It must shape the reasoning, not appear only in an ornamental concession.
concepts.insight: Ask what your position gains and what it puts at risk. Develop that tension with evidence while still making a judgment.
concepts.example: Preserving a person’s story may serve public memory while threatening that person’s control over disclosure.
concepts.misconception: A single “although” sentence or elaborate vocabulary does not automatically earn sophistication.

project.title: The unresolved-tension triptych
project.brief: Create a work that makes two legitimate values difficult to reconcile.
project.composition: Write two strong perspectives and a third position that makes a reasoned, limited choice.
project.visual: Design a triptych whose panels connect without visually erasing their disagreement.
project.analysis: Analyze the rhetorical cost of your final compromise.
project.argument: Defend the decision while identifying the value it cannot fully protect.
project.reflection: What remains unresolved after your most careful argument?

practice.passage: Original fictional argument: “An archive should preserve testimony, yet contributors should retain control over disclosure. Delayed access can protect privacy now while preserving a record for future study, though some present questions will remain unanswered.”

read.stem: The argument develops complexity by
options: using a difficult word without explanation.
weighing two values and acknowledging the cost of its compromise.
avoiding any recommendation.
declaring both values meaningless.
rationales: The reasoning, not vocabulary, creates complexity.
Delayed access protects privacy but limits immediate research.
It proposes delayed access.
Both are treated as important.

write.stem: Which addition most productively extends the tension?
options: The delay should be negotiated with contributors because different disclosures carry different risks.
This is a complex issue.
Privacy and research are always identical.
Everyone should simply agree.
rationales: This specifies how the compromise must respond to varied stakes.
Naming complexity does not develop it.
This erases the tension.
Agreement is asserted without reasoning.

frq.prompt: Communities benefit from preserving personal histories, but individuals may wish to keep parts of their lives private. Develop an argument about how public memory should be balanced with individual control.
frq.focus: Let a tension shape the argument rather than appear only in its opening.

concepts.title: Fallacies & faulty inference
concepts.definition: A fallacy is a defect in reasoning, not merely an unpopular conclusion. Common problems include false dilemmas, unsupported causal claims, distorted opposition, and generalizations beyond the evidence.
concepts.insight: Describe the actual inferential failure before naming it. Repair the argument if possible; a label alone does not explain why the conclusion lacks support.
concepts.example: “Fund this plan or abandon all learning” excludes other ways to support learning.
concepts.misconception: An emotionally expressed claim is not automatically fallacious.

project.title: The argument repair clinic
project.brief: Turn flawed public reasoning into a defensible argument.
project.composition: Write a deliberately flawed fictional editorial and a repaired version with an audit.
project.visual: Create diagnostic cards showing the broken inference and its repair.
project.analysis: Explain the specific failure without attacking the person who might make it.
project.argument: Defend which revised claims survive and which must be abandoned.
project.reflection: Did identifying a flaw tempt you to dismiss evidence that was still useful?

practice.passage: Original fictional editorial: “Either we adopt this exact tutoring plan or we do not care about students.”

read.stem: The reasoning is flawed because it
options: mentions students.
uses a short sentence.
excludes other ways to care about students.
contains a recommendation.
rationales: The subject is not the logical problem.
Length does not create the false choice.
The statement treats one plan and indifference as the only possibilities.
Recommendations can be reasonable.

write.stem: Which revision best repairs the argument?
options: Remove the word “students.”
Compare this plan with other tutoring options using access, quality, and cost.
Anyone who disagrees is worse than uncaring.
Repeat the original claim more confidently.
rationales: A word deletion does not repair the false dilemma.
The revision restores relevant alternatives and criteria.
The attack intensifies the same flaw.
Confidence does not supply alternatives or evidence.

frq.prompt: Debates are often framed as a choice between two extremes. Develop an argument about the value and limitations of seeking alternatives to those extremes.
frq.focus: Avoid treating compromise as automatically correct; evaluate the available choices.

concepts.title: Limitations & uncertainty
concepts.definition: A limitation identifies where evidence, method, scope, or implementation constrains a conclusion. Acknowledging uncertainty should inform the level of confidence and the next action.
concepts.insight: Distinguish “we do not know” from “nothing can be known.” Specify which uncertainty matters to the decision and what would reduce it.
concepts.example: A four-day observation can justify further inquiry without settling a year-round construction decision.
concepts.misconception: Uncertainty does not mean every interpretation is equally supported.

project.title: The uncertainty observatory
project.brief: Design a decision that remains responsible under incomplete knowledge.
project.composition: Write a recommendation, an uncertainty register, and a revision under a changed assumption.
project.visual: Build a map showing high-confidence findings, unresolved questions, and decision thresholds.
project.analysis: Analyze how each uncertainty affects the recommendation.
project.argument: Defend what can be done now and what requires more evidence.
project.reflection: Which unknown mattered less than you initially believed?

practice.passage: Original fictional report: “The pilot was observed only on dry Saturdays. It supports further testing, but it cannot tell us how the space functions on wet weekdays.”

read.stem: The limitation concerns chiefly
options: proof that the data were fabricated.
the impossibility of learning anything.
the precision of the method used to count individual visits.
the conditions represented by the observations.
rationales: No fabrication is alleged.
The report supports further testing.
The passage limits the conditions sampled; it does not identify a counting error or precision problem.
Weather and day of week restrict generalization.

write.stem: Which next step best addresses the limitation?
options: Collect more observations on the same dry Saturdays only.
Remove the limitation from the report.
Observe use across weather conditions and weekdays before making a broad claim.
Declare that all days are identical.
rationales: This may add data without addressing the key scope limit.
Omission conceals rather than resolves uncertainty.
The additional sampling targets the missing conditions.
The assumption ignores the gap.

frq.prompt: Decisions often must be made before all relevant information is available. Develop an argument about how uncertainty should influence the timing and scope of action.
frq.focus: Identify a decision-relevant uncertainty and a proportionate response.

concepts.title: Transfer across contexts
concepts.definition: Transfer is the use of a learned principle in a new situation. It requires recognizing both a relevant similarity and the differences that demand adaptation.
concepts.insight: Name the principle you are carrying over, then test its boundary. A strategy effective in one setting may fail when audience, power, or stakes change.
concepts.example: A playful satire for peers may need a different form when addressed to people directly harmed by the policy.
concepts.misconception: Reusing a successful template is not the same as transferring judgment.

project.title: The traveling argument
project.brief: Move an argument into a situation that resists its original form.
project.composition: Adapt a school-policy argument for a community organization with different resources and authority.
project.visual: Create a travel map showing what crosses contexts and what must be redesigned.
project.analysis: Explain three successful transfers and two necessary changes.
project.argument: Defend the adapted proposal using the new situation’s constraints.
project.reflection: Which apparent similarity concealed the most consequential difference?

practice.passage: Original fictional reflection: “Our club’s anonymous suggestion box worked because members trusted the moderator. A townwide version would need a clear review process before we could expect similar trust.”

read.stem: The reflection recognizes that transfer depends on
options: recreating or replacing a condition that supported the original success.
assuming all groups are identical.
abandoning every lesson from the club.
preserving the original group’s small membership size.
rationales: Trust in moderation may not automatically carry to the larger setting.
The writer identifies a changed condition.
The lesson informs the new design.
The reflection proposes a townwide version and identifies moderation, not identical group size, as the condition to address.

write.stem: Which addition best develops the adaptation?
options: Use the same box and assume trust will follow.
Declare every complaint invalid.
Avoid explaining the process.
Publish moderation criteria and a process for challenging decisions.
rationales: The physical object does not reproduce the social condition.
This undermines the purpose.
Opacity does not address the identified need.
These steps address trust in a less familiar setting.

frq.prompt: A successful practice in one community may be adopted elsewhere. Develop an argument about the extent to which local context should shape the adoption of successful models.
frq.focus: Explain both the transferable principle and the necessary adaptation.

concepts.title: Reflection & metacognition
concepts.definition: Reflection examines how decisions, evidence, feedback, and revision changed your understanding. Metacognition makes your own reasoning available for inspection and improvement.
concepts.insight: Use before-and-after evidence. Explain why a choice changed and identify a principle you could test in a future task.
concepts.example: “I narrowed ‘all students’ after comparing schedules” explains a decision; “I learned a lot” does not.
concepts.misconception: Reflection is not simply a report of effort or enjoyment.

project.title: The revision field journal
project.brief: Document learning as a sequence of decisions.
project.composition: Collect a draft, feedback, revision, and a reflective essay tracing three changed judgments.
project.visual: Create a field journal with annotated before-and-after excerpts and a map of remaining questions.
project.analysis: Distinguish changes caused by evidence from changes made for audience response.
project.argument: Defend one principle you will carry into a new assignment.
project.reflection: What evidence would show that your new principle needs revision?

practice.passage: Original fictional reflection: “I replaced ‘all residents’ with ‘residents arriving after six’ because the interviews involved only evening users. The change made my claim narrower and more supportable.”

read.stem: The reflection is substantive because it
options: substitutes praise for analysis.
connects a specific revision to an evidentiary limit.
reports only that the writer worked hard.
claims no further revision is possible.
rationales: It analyzes a decision rather than praising it.
It identifies the change, reason, and consequence.
Effort is not its focus.
No such claim appears.

write.stem: Which addition best extends the reflection toward future learning?
options: Next time I will compare the population in my evidence with the population named in my claim.
My essay is now perfect.
My revised sentence was shorter than the original sentence.
Next time I will avoid interviews so that my claims need no limits.
rationales: The sentence turns the experience into a transferable check.
The absolute judgment lacks support.
Length describes a surface change without establishing a principle for future evidentiary judgments.
Avoiding one source type does not remove the need to match claims to evidence.

frq.prompt: Reflecting on an experience can alter what a person learns from it. Develop an argument about the value of deliberate reflection in improving judgment.
frq.focus: Use concrete evidence of changed decisions, not general claims about growth.

concepts.title: Multimodal composition & ethical design
concepts.definition: Multimodal composition coordinates prose, image, layout, sound, or movement to make meaning. Each mode should do purposeful work while preserving factual integrity and access to the argument.
concepts.insight: Explain what the visual contributes beyond decoration. Provide a text equivalent, distinguish invention from evidence, and evaluate what the medium makes easy to overlook.
concepts.example: A map can expose a spatial barrier while an accompanying paragraph explains the policy causing it.
concepts.misconception: Artistic polish is not a substitute for an accurate, defensible argument.

project.title: The counter-perspective atlas: capstone
project.brief: Create an integrated rhetorical atlas inspired by the supplied project.
project.composition: Compose three original texts of 500–700 words on one enduring controversy, each with a defensible position and a defined audience. Select style according to purpose, not ideological stereotype.
project.visual: Build a codex, map, or interactive triptych; provide accessible descriptions and a source key.
project.analysis: Write 900–1,200 words of commentary analyzing textual and visual choices, plausible effects, and a failed alternative.
project.argument: Write a 700–900 word position essay responding to the strongest claims across your atlas.
project.reflection: Which perspective changed your position, which visual choice changed your reasoning, and which tension remains unresolved?

practice.passage: Original fictional project description: An atlas presents three views on public memory. Its map shows which voices appear in an archive; annotations explain omissions, and a text version describes the same relationships.

read.stem: The visual is most rhetorically useful when it
options: presents invented statistics as historical fact.
prevents readers from accessing the prose.
makes relationships among inclusion, omission, and power inspectable.
replaces every explanation with decoration.
rationales: That would misrepresent evidence.
Obstruction undermines the composition’s purpose.
The map contributes an argument through spatial relations.
Decoration alone does not communicate the reasoning.

write.stem: Which revision best strengthens the project’s intellectual rigor?
options: Make the opposing view intentionally foolish.
Explain how the map’s categories were chosen and include a case that complicates them.
Give each perspective the same amount of visual space regardless of its evidence.
Delete all source information.
rationales: Caricature weakens the comparison and argument.
The revision makes the design’s assumptions and limits visible.
Equal space can imply equal support; it does not examine whether the underlying categories and claims are warranted.
This prevents readers from tracing support.

frq.prompt: Visual forms can make complex arguments accessible, but they can also simplify away important tensions. Develop an argument about the responsibilities of creators who communicate complex issues through visual media.
frq.focus: Evaluate the relationship between clarity, persuasion, and intellectual honesty.

concepts.title: Stasis & locating disagreement
concepts.definition: Stasis is a way to locate what an argument is actually disputing. A useful set of questions concerns facts, definitions, evaluation, and action: what happened, what kind of issue it is, how it should be judged, and what should follow.
concepts.insight: Map which propositions participants share and which remain contested. A new statistic may not resolve a disagreement over values, and a policy recommendation may arrive before participants agree on the problem. Use the questions flexibly rather than as a compulsory essay sequence.
concepts.example: Two readers can agree that attendance fell while disagreeing about whether that decline indicates failure and whether cancellation is justified.
concepts.misconception: Disagreement does not always come from missing facts. Identifying a shared factual claim can reveal a deeper disagreement about definitions, standards, or remedies.

project.title: The disagreement map room
project.brief: Design a deliberation that helps participants address the same question.
project.composition: Choose a contested school decision. Write three 350-word stakeholder statements, each grounded in a common evidence dossier and a distinct, explicitly stated concern. Create a moderator’s memo locating agreements and unresolved questions.
project.visual: Build a floor plan with rooms for factual, definitional, evaluative, and policy questions. Place statements where their disagreement belongs and provide a text route through the map.
project.analysis: Analyze six choices that either clarify the dispute or make speakers talk past one another. Explain how your arrangement affects which question seems most urgent.
project.argument: Recommend the next question the group should investigate, using specific evidence from the statements. Address why beginning with the final policy might be attractive, then revise the moderator’s memo after a mock discussion or self-review.
project.reflection: Which apparent conflict disappeared when you separated agreement about events from disagreement about what those events mean?

practice.passage: Original fictional committee exchange: “Both speakers accepted that attendance at the festival had fallen. One called the festival unsuccessful because it no longer drew a large crowd. The other called it successful because the smaller workshops allowed longer conversations. The chair asked for another attendance count. That count might settle the number, but the speakers already agreed on the decline; they differed about what the festival should accomplish.”

read.stem: The passage suggests that the speakers’ central disagreement concerns
options: whether the attendance records show a decline.
which speaker is authorized to count workshop participants.
whether the festival occurred in the same location as last year.
the criteria by which the festival’s success should be evaluated.
rationales: The first sentence states that both speakers accept the decline.
No disagreement about counting authority appears.
The passage provides no dispute about location.
They accept the decline but weigh crowd size and sustained conversation differently.

write.stem: The writer wants to propose a next step that addresses the actual disagreement. Which addition best develops that reasoning?
options: The committee should interview only people who stayed away to determine whether the festival failed.
The committee should assume that any smaller event must be less successful.
The committee should clarify whether reach, depth of participation, or a combination of the two best serves the festival’s purpose.
The committee should repeat the count until both speakers accept that attendance fell.
rationales: Absence may provide useful evidence about reach, but it cannot alone settle whether depth of participation also counts as success.
This adopts one speaker’s disputed criterion without defending it.
The proposal addresses the conflicting standards rather than recounting an accepted fact.
Both already accept the decline; repetition would not resolve the evaluative dispute.

frq.prompt: People sometimes respond to a disagreement by supplying more facts, even when the dispute concerns definitions or values. Write an essay that argues your position on what makes a response to disagreement productive.
frq.focus: Use specific cases to distinguish a lack of information from a conflict in standards or purposes.

concepts.title: Ethical representation
concepts.definition: Ethical representation gives other people’s positions and experiences enough context to be understood accurately, including qualifications that complicate the writer’s own argument. It distinguishes evidence from inference and avoids treating one voice as a substitute for an entire group.
concepts.insight: Ask whose words you select, which conditions you omit, and what your framing invites readers to infer. Strong disagreement can remain fair: present the version an informed opponent could recognize before explaining its limits.
concepts.example: Quoting a resident’s support for a trial while deleting the condition that made that support possible can reverse the practical meaning of the statement.
concepts.misconception: Fairness does not require equal space for every claim or treating all evidence as equally sound. It requires accurate context and justified distinctions.

project.title: The editorial responsibility desk
project.brief: Publish a defensible account of a disagreement without turning people into symbols.
project.composition: Use a supplied passage or a clearly fictional dossier containing at least three qualified positions. Write a 600-word feature and a 350-word editorial that disagrees with one position. Keep a quotation and context log; do not invent testimony from real people.
project.visual: Design an annotated publication spread showing quote selection, caption context, and omitted material. Provide a text-only edition with the same qualifications.
project.analysis: Analyze six framing decisions across the feature and editorial. Explain who gains apparent authority or loses nuance through each choice, including the visual hierarchy.
project.argument: Defend the editorial’s judgment against the strongest accurately represented objection. Conduct a context audit, then revise two passages where selection made the evidence seem more certain or representative than it was.
project.reflection: Which edit made your argument less convenient but more accountable to the evidence?

practice.passage: Original fictional interview and editorial draft: A resident says, “I support the night market if the town keeps a quiet route home and reviews the noise after the trial. Without those protections, I would oppose it.” An editorial quotes only “I support the night market” and introduces the resident as evidence that nearby households have accepted the plan. The editor has interviewed no other household.

read.stem: The editorial’s treatment of the interview is most misleading because it
options: removes conditions essential to the resident’s support and treats one interview as a broader consensus.
uses a direct quotation instead of a paraphrase.
identifies a resident as someone affected by the proposal.
describes the market as a plan before the trial has ended.
rationales: The quotation loses its explicit limits, while the framing expands one person’s position to households generally.
Direct quotation is not inherently misleading; selection and framing create the distortion.
That context can be relevant and is not the source of the misrepresentation.
The passage does not suggest that “plan” misstates the proposal’s stage.

write.stem: Which revision most accurately represents the available evidence while still acknowledging support?
options: Nearby households support the market, although some details may still need attention.
The resident opposed the market because noise might become a problem.
The resident’s enthusiasm proves that a noise review will be unnecessary.
One interviewed resident supported a trial conditional on a quiet route home and a review of noise; the interview does not establish a neighborhood consensus.
rationales: The sentence retains an unsupported consensus and reduces essential conditions to vague details.
This removes the resident’s conditional support rather than representing it.
The source explicitly requires a review; the revision reverses that condition.
The revision preserves the conditions and limits the population to the evidence available.

frq.prompt: A writer must select and arrange other people’s words to make an argument, but selection can distort the positions being represented. Write an essay that argues your position on the obligations of a writer who uses individual testimony to support a public claim.
frq.focus: Develop criteria for preserving context, acknowledging limits, and making justified inferences.
